**WORKING PAPER**

**Excise, Externalities and Pathways**

*A three-part diagnostic for country fiscal teams*

*Combining a structured reading of the excise schedule (Part A) with a standardised health-and-climate externality diagnostic (Part B) and a synthesised policy-pathway analysis (Part C), this paper proposes a recurring institutional product that joins instrument-level legibility to system-level externality reasoning. It harmonises inputs from CPAT, the Climate and Health Program, the IMF Getting Energy Prices Right framework, and country excise schedules into one document a finance minister can read and act on.*

**World Bank**

Draft for discussion · May 2026

# Executive Summary

Finance ministries in low- and middle-income countries make excise and fuel-tax decisions on revenue and political grounds. Externality reasoning, when it appears at all, is brought in late and selectively. The analytical tools to do the job exist — excise schedules, CPAT, the Climate and Health Program, IMF Getting Energy Prices Right, country-level cost-benefit appraisal — but they sit in different silos and produce outputs at the wrong unit of analysis. No single product brings the parts together for a country team to use.

This paper proposes a recurring institutional product — an Excise-Externality-Pathways Diagnostic — built in three parts. It is not a new model and does not require new modelling capacity. It is a synthesis layer, and its headline output is a fiscal one: what excises raise now, what better design could raise, and the social costs that revenue also addresses.

## Purpose and the fiscal bottom line

The purpose of the diagnostic is to give a finance ministry a single, unified reading of its excise taxes — what they raise now, what they could raise under better design, and the social costs they do or do not address. Excise taxes play a corrective role: well-designed, they reduce economic distortions, sharpen price signals, **expand fiscal space and mobilise additional public revenue**. The diagnostic is built to make that revenue case explicit. For every priority line it estimates both **current revenue performance** and the **additional revenue potential** that improved design would unlock — so that the headline output a minister reads is a fiscal one: how much revenue a simple, efficient excise system can mobilise while also tackling social costs.

Framed this way, the three parts answer one fiscal question in sequence. **Part A** measures the revenue each line raises today and where erosion, gaps and anomalies are leaking it. **Part B** quantifies the revenue left on the table where externalities are underpriced — the implicit subsidy — and what closing the gap would yield. **Part C** converts those numbers into a sequenced reform calendar with a revenue trajectory a ministry can budget against. The social-cost case (health, climate, road safety) is real and is carried throughout, but the bottom line presented to decision-makers is fiscal: revenue mobilised, fiscal space created, and the cost of leaving the status quo in place.

**Scope and use.** The diagnostic covers all excises but concentrates analysis on six revenue-and-externality priority categories — fuel, vehicle, tobacco, alcohol, sugar-sweetened beverages and gambling. It is an automated, three-part report: Part A is already developed and demonstrated on two pilots, and the whole is designed to be tailored by country teams to the Public Finance Review (PFR) and country context. Beyond the written report, it **feeds the PFR Visualization tool with standardised data**, so the same harmonised measures support both the narrative a minister reads and the dashboards a country team maintains.

## The three parts

**Part A — Excise Diagnostic.** A structured reading of a country's excise schedule. Every line is categorised against a small typology (energy and environment; health — tobacco, alcohol, sugar-sweetened beverages; luxury; telecommunications and digital; financial transactions; industrial-input residuals; resource and extractive), recorded on five fields (item, current rate, structure, differentiation, recent changes), and scaled on three comparable measures: excise per standardised physical unit in US dollars; excise as a share of consumer price; and implied excise revenue as a share of GDP. The three measures are complementary — \$/unit is best for international comparison, % of consumer price for domestic policy debate, % of GDP for macro-fiscal framing — and together they triangulate the policy intensity of each line. The diagnostic is pre-analytical: it surfaces erosion, gaps and incoherence; it does not adjudicate whether rates are too high or too low.

**Part B — Health and Climate Externality Diagnostic.** A standardised seven-section assessment of how well the tax system handles transport-sector externalities — carbon emissions, local air pollution, road accidents, congestion, and road damage. The diagnostic takes outputs from CPAT and from the World Bank Climate and Health Program as inputs, applies a standardised valuation spine (a single value of statistical life, a single carbon shadow price, a single set of accident-cost parameters), and produces a country report with a fixed structure. Two tiers are proposed — a fuller version for capable LMICs and UMICs and a streamlined version for LICs — sharing a common spine. Part B also answers a sub-question the Part A approach cannot reach: what is the biggest externality not currently priced by the tax system?

**Part C — Policy Pathways.** A sequenced, country-specific reform pathway drawing on (i) the structural anomalies, gaps and erosion patterns surfaced by Part A; (ii) the externality-gap and incidence findings from Part B; (iii) international benchmarks and IMF Getting Energy Prices Right comparators; (iv) comparator-country success stories; and (v) a narrative political-economy analysis identifying which reforms are politically tractable, in what sequence, and with what compensation design. Part C does not duplicate the substantive findings of A and B; it draws them together and converts them into an actionable reform calendar.

## What Part A finds in the two pilot diagnostics

Worked diagnostics for Uganda (Excise Duty Act, 2014 as amended through 1 July 2025) and Sierra Leone (Excise Act, 1982 as amended through the Finance Act, 2026, effective 1 January 2026) demonstrate the framework. Aggregate priority-sector excise — energy, tobacco, alcohol and sugar-sweetened beverages combined — raises approximately 1.5 to 1.7 per cent of GDP in Uganda against 0.7 to 0.9 per cent in Sierra Leone. The gap is largely accounted for by fuel (about 1.3 per cent of GDP against 0.6 per cent). On rate intensity, Uganda runs roughly twice Sierra Leone on every priority measure: petrol excise at 30 per cent of pump price against 18 per cent; tobacco at 30 to 55 per cent of pack price against 10 to 15 per cent; beer at approximately USD 11 per litre of pure alcohol against approximately USD 7. Both countries sit well below international peers, with Sierra Leone further below.

Three anomalies emerge from the diagnostic that are invisible on the schedule itself. First, the Sierra Leonean wine schedule has not been redenominated since the 2022 Old Leone / New Leone conversion at 1,000 to 1; at face value wine is currently untaxed by excise at approximately USD 0.0002 per litre. This is almost certainly a drafting issue rather than an intended policy choice. Second, the Ugandan kerosene rate at UGX 200 per litre has been unchanged since 2018 and now stands at under 5 per cent of pump price. Third, both countries' specific rates show a clear erosion-and-restoration cycle visible only when the year-by-year trajectory is laid out — indexation is the obvious structural fix.

## What Part B contributes beyond Part A

Part A's by-instrument approach answers the question “is this line set correctly?”. It cannot answer “does the tax system as a whole deal with the externalities that matter?”. Part B does. Applied in a Tier 2 worked example for a stylised East African LIC, the diagnostic finds implicit subsidies — the undercharging of external costs — of approximately USD 410 million annually, exceeding direct fuel-tax revenue of USD 320 million. The largest implicit-subsidy components are local air pollution (43 per cent) and accidents (31 per cent). Diesel is substantially undertaxed; gasoline is roughly correctly taxed. This is a familiar pattern in developing-country settings.

Closing two-thirds of the diesel gap over three years would raise approximately USD 230 million annually — increasing total fuel-tax revenue by 70 per cent and approaching 1 per cent of GDP — with implicit-subsidy welfare gains larger still, because avoided health and accident costs accrue independently of revenue. With 30 per cent of the new revenue recycled into a flat per-household transfer, the bottom quintile is better off in net terms. Pedestrian fatalities account for nearly half of road deaths in the worked example; the accident externality is therefore a larger component of the total in LICs than in OECD applications, a structural finding that translates directly across countries.

## What Part C does with the findings

Part C draws Parts A and B together into a sequenced reform pathway. It does not generate new findings. It does three things the underlying diagnostics cannot.

**Sequencing.** Parts A and B both produce lists of policy candidates. They do not say which comes first. Part C sequences candidates by political tractability, fiscal yield, and administrative readiness — typically a three-year package with one anchor reform per year. The Tier 2 worked example sequences a USD 0.50 per litre diesel-tax closure over three steps, with the per-household transfer institutionalised in year two and a heavy-goods-vehicle distance charge scoped in year three.

**Comparator referencing.** Reform proposals carry more political weight when grounded in comparable experience. Rwanda, Ghana and Kenya have all raised diesel tax over the past decade in steps without macroeconomic disruption, particularly where reform was sequenced with targeted social protection. South Africa has the most developed legislative carbon-pricing architecture among middle-income countries. Chile, Colombia, Mexico and Brazil have institutionalised carbon components on fuels. Country teams need these references at hand when drafting reform proposals; Part C provides them.

**Political-economy analysis.** Reform proposals that survive contact with politics share recognisable features. In low- and middle-income countries with low per-capita motorisation and high pedestrian-fatality shares, the health and road-safety justification for fuel-tax reform polls substantially better than the climate justification. Local-content discounts in alcohol regimes produce rate inversions that create political winners and losers; redenomination anomalies persist because nobody loses from their persistence; tobacco rates are easier to raise in countries with low domestic production. Part C reads these dynamics from the schedule itself and proposes the sequencing that follows.

## The reform priorities the diagnostic identifies

Six reform priorities emerge from the combined diagnostic. They are listed in approximate order of political tractability rather than fiscal yield.

  -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  **Reform**                                         **Rationale**                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             **Fiscal yield**
  -------------------------------------------------- ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  **Redenomination of wine excise (Sierra Leone)**   FA2024 rates in Old Leones produce essentially zero excise after the 2022 redenomination. One-line schedule amendment in the next Finance Act. No constituency benefits from the anomaly.                                                                                                 Small. Wine consumption is low in Sierra Leone.

  **Indexation of specific rates**                   Both countries show clear erosion-and-restoration cycles. Indexation removes the political cost of restoration without losing real revenue. Standard reform.                                                                                                                              Material over time. Recovers the real value that drifts away between Finance Acts.

  **Sugar-content-graduated SSB excise**             Both countries are well below international peers on SSB taxation. UK and South Africa have demonstrated sugar-content differentiation can be designed and implemented. Strong public-health evidence.                                                                                    Moderate. Material in Uganda; smaller base in Sierra Leone.

  **Tobacco rate convergence**                       Both countries sit well below the WHO benchmark of 75 per cent of retail price as excise. Sierra Leone in particular has substantial headroom — a phased path of perhaps three Finance Acts at +30 per cent each would lift the country toward Uganda's lowest tier without disruption.   Moderate. Tobacco bases are small in both countries (smoking prevalence 4 to 5 per cent).

  **Diesel-tax closure of the externality gap**      Part B's central finding. Diesel is substantially undertaxed for air pollution and accidents. The fiscal-and-health argument is strong. Sequence with a flat per-household transfer to neutralise the regressivity.                                                                       Large. The diesel-gap closure in the Tier 2 worked example raises approximately 1 per cent of GDP.

  **Vehicle taxation reform**                        Vehicle taxation is structurally weak in both countries. Annual circulation levies are small or absent. Emissions-and-weight-graduated feebates address fleet composition without a Gruenspecht effect.                                                                                   Small at first; grows as the vehicle fleet expands.
  -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## How the diagnostic maps to the PFR

The diagnostic is designed to slot into the Public Finance Review (PFR) rather than to sit beside it. A generic PFR on excise taxation moves through a recognisable sequence of sections — health impact, identification and analysis of the tax structure, analysis of trends over time, benchmarking, and recommendations — with topics that are either required in every report or case-dependent on a country’s analytical capacity. The table below sets out that generic structure and distinguishes the topics that are always required from those that are added at an intermediate or advanced level of engagement. Part A of this diagnostic supplies the identification, trend and benchmarking rows; Part B supplies the health-impact, externality and distributional rows that the advanced column calls for; Part C supplies the recommendations and policy-simulation rows.

(\*) Scope, conflicts of interest, supply-side, tax-administration and distributional topics are treated qualitatively unless country data supports a fuller analysis. (\*\*) Consumption is reported where household-survey or sales data permit.*

## The key questions the diagnostic answers

The diagnostic is organised around a fixed set of key questions. Each part answers a distinct subset; together they move a country team from reading the schedule to acting on it. The questions are stated in full in the relevant sections of Parts A, B and C and consolidated here.

**Part A — Is each instrument set correctly?** What is in the schedule, how is each line structured, how intensely is it taxed on comparable measures, and where are the erosion, gaps and incoherence that the schedule hides?

**Part B — Does the tax system as a whole deal with the externalities that matter?** How do current excises compare with the social costs of the taxed goods — across both climate and health externalities — what is the biggest externality not currently priced, and who bears the burden of closing the gap?

**Part C — What should the country do, and in what order?** Which reforms are politically tractable, how should they be sequenced and compensated, and what comparator experience supports them?

***Key.** In spec: “Spec” = inherited from the climate and health programs’ existing capacities; “Added” = introduced by the diagnostic. Version: **Easy** = answerable in a simplified Part A from the schedule alone; **Comprehensive** = needs fuller data and integration with CPAT, the Climate & Health Program and IMF GEPR; **Both** = a core question deepened in the comprehensive version.*

## Why a synthesis layer is the contribution

The methodology to do this work in developing-country settings already exists. What is missing is the synthesis. CPAT produces high-quality estimates of mitigation, revenue, household incidence and macroeconomic effects across roughly two hundred countries — but CPAT is a model, not a report. The Climate and Health Program produces vulnerability assessments, mortality estimates and best-buy guidance — but at the sector rather than the system level. The IMF Getting Energy Prices Right work produces global estimates of corrective fuel-tax rates — but lacks the country-specific texture needed to defend a reform politically. Country transport teams produce project-level cost-benefit appraisal — at the wrong unit of analysis for fuel-tax design. Tax-policy teams produce revenue projections and tax-expenditure inventories — without externality reasoning. The Public Finance Review reads the excise schedule by instrument — without the system-level externality question.

The diagnostic does not duplicate any of these. It synthesises. The discipline is its main contribution: a single value of statistical life, a single carbon shadow price, a single set of accident-cost parameters, applied consistently across all the sectoral inputs in a single country, presented in a fixed-structure report that allows comparison across countries and incremental improvement of any single section without disturbing the rest.

Three practical steps would move the proposal from concept to product: a methodology note of perhaps thirty pages formalising the framework and fixing the default parameters; a fixed Word template populated from a common parameter spreadsheet; and two pilots — one Tier 1 (Colombia or Chile, both with strong analytical infrastructure) and one Tier 2 (Uganda fits existing World Bank engagement, and the Part A diagnostic is already drafted). Once the methodology and template are in place, a country team should be able to produce a draft report in two to three weeks using existing inputs rather than three months.

*The diagnostic does not require new institutional architecture. It sits between existing products as a synthesis layer.*

**PART A**

**Excise Diagnostic**

*A simple framework for reading a country's excise schedule, with worked diagnostics for Uganda and Sierra Leone*

# A1. What an excise diagnostic is, and what it is for

An excise diagnostic is a structured snapshot of a country's excise duty schedule, organised so that the schedule's underlying logic — and where that logic strains — becomes visible at a glance. It is not a revenue forecast, an incidence study, or a fiscal-impact assessment. It is a diagnostic in the medical sense: a clinician's first-pass examination, designed to surface what is there, what is missing, and what is moving.

Most excise schedules in low- and middle-income countries are accretive documents. They begin life narrow, organised around a small set of products that were easy to tax at the factory gate or the port a generation ago — alcohol, tobacco, fuel, perhaps a handful of luxury goods. They then grow line by line as Finance Ministries hunt for revenue, as health ministries push for tobacco and alcohol increases, as environment ministries discover plastics, and as digital and financial-services regulators try to drag mobile money and over-the-top services into the net. The result, after a decade or two of annual amendments, is a schedule that nobody fully owns and that few can read end-to-end.

The diagnostic addresses that legibility problem. It does five things.

**Categorises.** It groups every line in the schedule into a small set of policy categories — energy and environment, health (tobacco, alcohol, sugar-sweetened beverages), luxury, telecommunications, financial transactions, and industrial-input residuals. The categorisation forces an answer to the question “what is this excise for?” — a question schedules rarely answer for themselves.

**Standardises.** It records each line on a consistent set of dimensions: rate, structure (specific, ad valorem, hybrid), differentiation (by origin, content, user, ABV band), and recent changes. This makes the schedule comparable across countries, across time, and across categories.

**Surfaces erosion.** Specific rates that are not indexed to inflation lose real value year by year. The diagnostic tracks the catch-up amendments and makes the erosion-and-restoration cycle visible.

**Surfaces gaps.** When the typology is laid alongside the schedule, missing categories become obvious. A country with no plastics excise, no SSB excise, or no e-cigarette line in 2026 is making a policy choice — and the diagnostic puts that choice on the page.

**Surfaces incoherence.** Differentiation devices often accumulate without coordination. Local-content discounts, ABV bands, origin distinctions, user carve-outs — when stacked, they can produce rate inversions, arbitrage opportunities, and administrative friction. The diagnostic does not solve these problems but makes them visible.

The diagnostic is intentionally pre-analytical. It does not say whether a rate is too high or too low, whether a category is justified, or whether a reform is desirable. It produces a clean, comparable, structured representation of the schedule, on which subsequent analysis — revenue projections, incidence work, behavioural-response modelling, country-engagement advice — can build. In Hayek's sense, it is a way of organising tacit knowledge that already exists in the schedule but is not yet usable.

## Key questions Part A answers

*Part A is built to answer a short list of instrument-level questions. They are pre-analytical: each can be answered by reading and standardising the schedule, without modelling behaviour or adjudicating whether a rate is right.*

1.  **Coverage.** What does the schedule actually tax — which goods and services carry an excise, and which externality-relevant categories (carbon-bearing fuels, SSBs, plastics, e-cigarettes) are absent?

2.  **Structure.** Is each line specific, ad valorem or hybrid, and how is it differentiated — by origin, content, user or ABV band?

3.  **Intensity.** How heavily is each line taxed on three comparable measures — excise per standardised physical unit in US dollars, excise as a share of consumer price, and implied excise revenue as a share of GDP?

4.  **Benchmarking.** How do those intensities compare with regional peers, OECD averages and WHO or IMF reference levels?

5.  **Erosion.** Which specific rates are losing real value to inflation, and what is the erosion-and-restoration cycle when the year-by-year trajectory is laid out?

6.  **Coherence.** Where do differentiation devices — local-content discounts, ABV bands, origin distinctions — stack into rate inversions, arbitrage opportunities or administrative friction?

7.  **Price tracking.** For health-related products, how has the excise-inclusive price moved relative to general CPI inflation and to household incomes — a measure of whether taxes are keeping pace and continuing to discourage consumption?

The price-tracking question (Q7) is shared with the health program, which routinely compares the price of health-related products with CPI inflation and with household incomes. The climate program holds the equivalent data for fuels but does not yet report it; bringing the two onto the same affordability measure is one of the concrete gains from a joint offering.

# A2. Three measures for comparability

The schedule on its own — a list of rates, in local-currency units, against locally defined products — is not directly comparable across countries, across time, or across sectors. To make excise lines comparable, this paper uses three measures that scale each rate in a different way.

### A2.1 Excise per standardised physical unit (USD)

The rate, converted to US dollars, expressed per physical unit appropriate to the line: per litre for fuel, per litre of pure alcohol for alcoholic beverages, per pack of 20 sticks for cigarettes, per kilogram for cement and tobacco leaf. This is the most robust comparator and the easiest to cross-reference against international benchmarks (OECD averages, regional peers, WHO recommendations). It is unaffected by the differentiation structure — a hybrid higher-of rate is converted to the binding rate at typical product prices, an ABV-banded rate is evaluated at a representative ABV — and so cuts through architectural differences between schedules. Its weakness is that it loses information about whether the rate is specific or ad valorem, which matters for inflation behaviour.

### A2.2 Excise as a percentage of consumer price

The rate divided by the typical retail price of the taxed good — pump price for fuel, retail pack price for cigarettes, retail bottle price for alcohol and SSBs. This measure speaks directly to affordability and to pass-through: it is the share of what the consumer pays that goes to excise. It is the standard health-policy comparator (the WHO benchmark for tobacco is at least 75 per cent of retail price as excise) and the standard energy-policy comparator (OECD fuel excise typically runs 30 to 50 per cent of pump price). Its weakness is that it depends on the chosen reference price, which moves materially within a year, between regions of a country, and between branded and unbranded segments.

### A2.3 Implied excise revenue as a percentage of GDP

Rate multiplied by estimated annual consumption volume, divided by nominal GDP. This is the macroeconomic comparator — the measure that tells the Finance Ministry how much revenue the line generates relative to the size of the economy. It is the most informative measure for international fiscal comparisons (regional excise revenue ratios, IMF tax-effort benchmarks) but also the most error-prone, because it depends on consumption volumes that are usually not published at the tariff-line level. Implied figures are sensitive to volume assumptions; ranges are reported where the volume is uncertain. Where reported revenue is available, it should be preferred over implied figures; this paper uses implied figures throughout because line-level revenue is not published in either Uganda or Sierra Leone.

The three measures are complementary. The \$/unit measure is best for international comparison; the % of consumer price measure is best for domestic policy debate; the % of GDP measure is best for macro-fiscal framing. Read together they triangulate the policy intensity of an excise line: a rate that looks low in \$/unit terms but high in % of consumer price terms tells a different story than one that looks the opposite way around.

# A3. Methodology

### A3.1 Coverage

The diagnostic covers two countries — Uganda and Sierra Leone — at a single point in time, the law in force on 27 April 2026. For Uganda this is the Excise Duty Act, 2014 as amended through the Excise Duty (Amendment) Acts (No. 1) and (No. 2), 2025, both effective from 1 July 2025. The Excise Duty (Amendment) Bill, 2026 had been passed by Parliament but, as of the cut-off date, had not received presidential assent and is therefore not in force. For Sierra Leone the position is the Excise Act, 1982 as amended through the Finance Act, 2026 — assented on 29 December 2025, gazetted 7 January 2026, effective from 1 January 2026.

Within each schedule, every excisable line is included. Where lines have been administratively grouped (e.g. tobacco substitutes alongside cigars), the grouping in the schedule is preserved. The diagnostic also notes adjacent fiscal instruments that function as excises in economic substance — Sierra Leone's regulatory cellular levy under the Finance Act, 2023, and the FA2026 vehicle annual circulation levy — even where they sit outside the Excise Act.

### A3.2 Typology

Each line is assigned to one of seven categories: energy and environment; health (tobacco, alcohol, sugar-sweetened beverages); luxury; telecommunications and digital; financial transactions; industrial-input and “nuisance” residuals; and resource / extractive. The categorisation is by stated or implicit policy rationale, not by HS code or schedule placement. Lines that could fit two categories are assigned to the dominant rationale (a vehicle registration levy goes under transport / energy rather than under luxury; a gambling excise goes under health rather than under luxury). A small number of lines — procedural framework provisions, payment-window rules — are categorised separately as “procedural”.

### A3.3 Recording each line

Each line is recorded on five fields: category (per the typology above); item (the name of the excisable good or service as it appears in the schedule); current rate (in local currency units, at the cut-off date); structure and differentiation (specific / ad valorem / hybrid; differentiation by origin, content, user, ABV band, etc.); and recent changes (the trajectory of the line since 2020, with each amendment cycle noted, plus any pending bill).

### A3.4 Computing the three measures

#### Currency conversion

Rates are converted to US dollars at working exchange rates: UGX 3,750 per USD for Uganda, NLe 22 per USD for Sierra Leone. Both are mid-rates in force around the cut-off date and align with central-bank reference rates within plus or minus 3 per cent. Sierra Leone redenominated the Leone in April 2022 at 1,000 Old Leones to 1 New Leone; rates quoted in the schedule in Old Leones (Le) are converted on the assumption that the redenomination has not yet been formally applied to those lines (so Le X per litre is treated as nominally NLe X / 1,000 per litre and explicitly flagged where the result is anomalous).

#### Standardising physical units

Where the schedule uses a non-standard unit, the rate is converted to a standard one. Cigarettes per 1,000 sticks are converted to per pack of 20 (multiply by 0.02). Specific alcohol rates per litre of product are converted to per litre of pure alcohol (LPA) by dividing by the representative ABV (5 per cent for beer, 12 per cent for wine, 40 per cent for spirits). Hybrid higher-of rates are evaluated at a representative product price and the binding component reported.

#### Reference prices for the % of consumer price measure

Consumer prices are taken from the most recent published source closest to the cut-off date. Fuel pump prices: Uganda UGX 5,244 per litre petrol (GlobalPetrolPrices, 20 April 2026); Sierra Leone NLe 28 per litre petrol and diesel (PRA, September 2024) and NLe 27.4 per litre diesel (approximately USD 1.39) (GlobalPetrolPrices, November 2025). Cigarette pack prices: Ugandan retail prices estimated at UGX 4,000 to 6,000 per pack of 20 depending on brand and pack type; Sierra Leonean retail estimated at NLe 22 per pack. Alcohol and SSB retail prices: estimated from market surveys and import data; the figures are best-estimate ranges rather than point estimates.

#### Volumes for the implied revenue measure

Consumption volumes are taken from the most recent published industry or regulator source. Fuel: Uganda approximately 2.5 billion litres total petroleum imports per year (UNOC, 2024), with monthly demand around 240 million litres growing 7 per cent per annum; April 2026 import plan 283 million litres petrol plus 180 million diesel plus 25 million Jet A1. The petrol / diesel split is taken at roughly the import-plan ratio (60 / 40 for petrol against diesel). Sierra Leone approximately 524 million litres total petroleum sales (PRA, 2023), assumed to have grown approximately 10 per cent to approximately 575 million by 2026; petrol / diesel split assumed roughly 50 / 50 in the absence of a published breakdown. Cigarettes: Uganda smoking prevalence 4.4 per cent among adults aged 15 and over (WHO, 2024), giving approximately 1.2 million smokers; assumed average consumption around 10 sticks per day (consistent with regional estimates) gives approximately 4.4 billion sticks per year. Sierra Leone has no domestic tobacco production — all consumption is imported — and prevalence is reported in older sources at 3 to 5 per cent of adults, giving approximately 120 to 200 thousand smokers and approximately 0.5 to 1.0 billion sticks per year. Alcohol: WHO Global Status Report on Alcohol estimates Uganda total adult per-capita consumption at approximately 9.5 litres of pure alcohol per year (mostly opaque beer); Sierra Leone approximately 6.7 LPA per year (mostly informal and home-brewed). Volumes captured by the formal excise net are a fraction of these — perhaps 30 to 40 per cent — and figures should be read with that in mind. SSBs: no published volume data for either country; figures here are best-effort estimates based on import data and assumed per-capita consumption.

#### GDP denominator

Working figures: Uganda USD 55 billion (between World Bank 2024 of USD 53.65 billion and FocusEconomics 2024 estimate of USD 56.6 billion); Sierra Leone USD 7.5 billion (between World Bank 2024 of USD 7.0 billion and IMF 2026 projection of USD 8.27 billion). The IMF's higher 2026 figure for Uganda (USD 73 billion) is treated as overstated and not used. Using larger GDP figures would proportionally lower the implied per cent of GDP estimates.

### A3.5 Limitations and what the diagnostic does not do

Five caveats. First, the implied per cent of GDP figures are approximations within a factor of perhaps 1.5x, due to volume uncertainty. Reported revenue figures, when available, should always be preferred. Second, the per cent of consumer price figures move materially with the chosen reference price; ranges are used where appropriate. Third, the diagnostic does not model behavioural response — pass-through, demand elasticity, evasion — so figures are static. Fourth, informal-sector and home-produced goods (opaque beer, akpeteshi, untaxed cigarettes from neighbouring countries) are largely outside the formal excise net and so the diagnostic understates the alcohol and tobacco footprint of consumption while accurately representing the formal-sector excise base. Fifth, the diagnostic surfaces but does not adjudicate policy choices: it does not say whether a rate is too high or too low, whether a category is justified, or whether a reform is desirable.

# A4. Results

The full diagnostics — every line in each schedule, on the five fields described above — are presented in Appendix A. The year-by-year trajectory of those rates from 2020 to the current law is in Appendix B. The worked computations of the three comparable measures, line by line, are presented in section A5 below. This section reports the headline findings.

### A4.1 Energy and vehicles

On the \$/unit measure, Uganda's headline fuel excise is roughly twice Sierra Leone's (USD 0.41 against USD 0.23 per litre on petrol; USD 0.33 against USD 0.23 on diesel). On the per cent of consumer price measure, the gap is similar (approximately 30 per cent against 18 per cent on petrol). Sierra Leonean pump prices are higher in dollar terms because of higher landed costs, not higher tax. On the implied per cent of GDP measure, fuel excise raises an order of magnitude more in Uganda — roughly 1.3 per cent of GDP combined across petrol and diesel, against 0.6 per cent of GDP in Sierra Leone. The gap reflects both the higher rate and Uganda's larger fuel volume relative to the size of the economy.

For international context, OECD-average fuel excise is USD 0.55 per litre on petrol, 30 to 50 per cent of pump price, and 1.5 to 2.5 per cent of GDP. South Africa runs USD 0.20 to 0.25 per litre. Both Uganda and Sierra Leone are within the lower-middle-income range, with Uganda closer to OECD intensity than Sierra Leone.

Vehicle taxation is structurally weak in both countries. Uganda has a one-off motorcycle first registration charge of UGX 200,000 (USD 53) that has been stable since 2018 and is proposed to rise to UGX 500,000 in the 2026 Bill. Sierra Leone introduced an annual circulation levy in FA2026 (NLe 500 / USD 23 for cars, trucks and buses; NLe 200 / USD 9 for motorbikes; USD 500 to 1,000 for vessels). Neither rises above 0.05 per cent of GDP.

### A4.2 Health — tobacco

Uganda's structure produces a much heavier excise burden than Sierra Leone's. The lowest Ugandan tier (USD 0.35 per pack on locally manufactured soft cap cigarettes) is 2.5 times the single Sierra Leonean rate (USD 0.14 per pack); the highest Ugandan tier (USD 1.07 per pack on imported hinge lid) is 7.5 times. On the per cent of retail measure, Uganda runs 30 to 55 per cent against Sierra Leone's 10 to 15 per cent. Both countries are well below the WHO benchmark of at least 75 per cent of retail price as excise.

On revenue, tobacco excise is small in both countries — 0.05 to 0.10 per cent of GDP in Uganda, approximately 0.02 per cent of GDP in Sierra Leone — reflecting modest smoking prevalence (4.4 per cent in Uganda; estimated similar in Sierra Leone) more than the rate level. South Africa raises approximately 0.4 per cent of GDP from tobacco excise; the EU average is approximately 0.6 per cent. There is meaningful headroom for further increases in both countries, particularly Sierra Leone.

### A4.3 Health — alcohol

On like-for-like beer (approximately 5 per cent ABV), Uganda's malt beer rate (approximately USD 11 per litre of pure alcohol) is approximately 50 per cent higher than Sierra Leone's strictest band (D4, approximately USD 7 per LPA), and several multiples above the local-content-discounted bands in either country. Both are well below OECD benchmarks of USD 15 to 40 per LPA on beer.

**Redenomination anomaly.** The diagnostic surfaces a redenomination anomaly in the Sierra Leonean wine schedule. FA2024 set wine excise at Le 4.20 to 22 per litre depending on ABV band and origin, in Old Leones. After the April 2022 redenomination at 1,000 Old Le to 1 NLe, those rates would translate to NLe 0.0042 to 0.022 per litre — roughly USD 0.0002 to 0.001 per litre, which is essentially zero. The schedule has not been formally restated through two subsequent Finance Acts (FA2025, FA2026). At face value, wine in Sierra Leone is currently untaxed by excise. This is almost certainly a drafting issue rather than an intended policy choice; remediation is a one-line schedule amendment.

Alcohol excise revenue is approximately 0.2 per cent of GDP in Uganda and 0.05 per cent in Sierra Leone, reflecting both lower rates and the larger informal / home-brewed share of the Sierra Leonean market that sits outside the formal excise net. OECD averages run 0.4 to 0.6 per cent of GDP.

### A4.4 Health — sugar-sweetened beverages

Both countries are weak on SSBs. Uganda taxes all non-alcoholic beverages including juice at a flat 12 per cent or UGX 250 per litre — no sugar-content differentiation. Sierra Leone taxes only energy drinks (20 per cent) and imported juice (20 per cent), leaving general soft drinks essentially untaxed. The UK soft drinks industry levy by comparison is GBP 0.18 to 0.24 per litre depending on sugar content (approximately USD 0.23 to 0.30); Mexico's SSB excise is approximately USD 0.05 per litre flat; South Africa's Health Promotion Levy is ZAR 0.0221 per gram of sugar above 4g/100ml. On either the per-litre or per cent of retail measure, both countries tax SSBs less heavily than peers.

### A4.5 Aggregate picture

Combining the priority sectors: Uganda's energy plus tobacco plus alcohol plus SSB excise raises approximately 1.5 to 1.7 per cent of GDP; Sierra Leone's raises approximately 0.7 to 0.9 per cent of GDP. The gap is largely accounted for by fuel (approximately 1.3 per cent against approximately 0.6 per cent) — the other categories raise broadly comparable shares of GDP. Adding cement, gambling and the regulatory cellular levies in Sierra Leone narrows the gap modestly but does not close it.

On rate intensity, Uganda is closer to international benchmarks across the board. Fuel: 30 per cent of pump price against 18 per cent. Tobacco: 30 to 55 per cent of pack price against 10 to 15 per cent. Beer: approximately USD 11 per LPA against approximately USD 7 per LPA on the highest-rate band. The ratio is roughly 2 to 1 in Uganda's favour on every measure. Both countries are below international peers, with Sierra Leone further below.

### A5.5 International benchmarks

For the comparable measures referenced in A4: OECD-average fuel excise USD 0.55 per litre on petrol, 30 to 50 per cent of pump price, 1.5 to 2.5 per cent of GDP; South Africa USD 0.20 to 0.25 per litre. WHO recommended tobacco excise at least 75 per cent of retail pack price; South Africa raises approximately 0.4 per cent of GDP from tobacco; EU approximately 0.6 per cent. OECD alcohol excise USD 15 to 40 per LPA on beer, USD 25 to 50 per LPA on spirits; OECD alcohol revenue 0.4 to 0.6 per cent of GDP. UK SDIL GBP 0.18 to 0.24 per litre (approximately USD 0.23 to 0.30) by sugar content; Mexico approximately USD 0.05 per litre flat; South Africa HPL ZAR 0.0221 per gram of sugar above 4g/100ml.

# A6. Part A conclusion

The diagnostic delivers three things that the schedule alone does not. First, a structured representation that is comparable across categories, across countries, and against international benchmarks. Second, a set of three scaled measures — \$/unit, per cent of consumer price, per cent of GDP — that triangulate the policy intensity of each excise line from complementary angles. Third, visibility on anomalies and gaps that are invisible on the schedule. The Sierra Leonean wine redenomination anomaly is the clearest example: the rates look normal in the schedule but compute to essentially zero once standardised. The Ugandan kerosene rate at UGX 200 per litre — unchanged since 2018 and now under 5 per cent of pump price — is another.

Three reform candidates emerge from the comparative measures rather than from the schedule itself. First, redenominate the Sierra Leonean wine schedule (one-line amendment in the next Finance Act). Second, introduce a sugar-content-graduated SSB excise in both countries — the rate gap to peers is largest here and the public-health rationale is well-evidenced. Third, lift Sierra Leonean cigarette excise from approximately USD 0.14 per pack toward Uganda's lowest tier (USD 0.35) — a phased path of perhaps three Finance Acts at plus 30 per cent each. None of these is on the immediate legislative horizon in either country, but all three are straightforward extensions of the existing schedule architecture rather than structural reforms. Part C of this paper picks up these candidates and develops them into a sequenced reform pathway, alongside the externality-driven candidates from Part B.

More broadly, the diagnostic suggests that the reform agenda in both countries is converging on a similar shape: indexation of specific rates to break the erosion-and-catch-up cycle visible in Appendix B; introduction of sugar-content-graduated SSB excise to plug the clearest gap relative to peers; and either explicit carbon-tax overlay on fuel or graduated emissions-based vehicle taxation to make environmental policy do work that fuel excise currently does only by accident.

The framework is replicable. Applied to a third country, the same five fields and three measures would produce a comparable diagnostic; applied to a region or a peer group, the framework would generate a multi-country comparative table on identical structure. The methodology is intentionally light: it is the discipline of consistent recording and consistent measurement, not a sophisticated analytical apparatus, that does the work.

**PART B**

**Health and Climate Externality Diagnostic**

*A standardised fuel and vehicle tax diagnostic for developing countries — integrating CPAT, health analysis and externality valuation in a UK-style appraisal format*

# B1. Purpose and Structure

## Purpose

Part A read the excise schedule by instrument: line by line, against a small typology, scaled on three measures. That approach answers the question “is this line set correctly?” — but it cannot answer the system-level question “does the tax system as a whole deal with the externalities that matter?”. Part B sets out a complementary diagnostic that does.

A finance ministry in a developing country setting fuel and vehicle tax rates faces the following question: what should our rates be, given what we know about carbon damages, local pollution mortality, road accidents, congestion, revenue needs, distributional incidence, and international norms? The question is well-defined. The answer requires data and judgement that span at least four ministries.

The current state of play. CPAT produces high-quality estimates of mitigation, revenue, household incidence, and macroeconomic effects of carbon-pricing and fuel-subsidy reforms across roughly two hundred countries. The Climate and Health Program produces vulnerability assessments, mortality estimates, and best-buy guidance. The IMF Getting Energy Prices Right work produces global estimates of corrective fuel-tax rates. Country transport teams produce project-level cost-benefit appraisal with their own values. Tax-policy teams produce revenue projections and tax-expenditure inventories.

None of these is the report a finance minister can read and act on. CPAT is a model, not a report. The Climate and Health Program outputs are sector-specific. Project cost-benefit appraisal is at the wrong unit of analysis. International benchmark estimates lack the country-specific texture needed to defend a reform politically. The result is that fuel-tax decisions in most developing countries are made on revenue and political grounds, with externality reasoning, when it appears at all, brought in late and selectively.

What a synthesis layer adds. The proposed Fuel and Vehicle Tax Diagnostic (FVTD) is a standard report — fixed structure, fixed valuation parameters, fixed comparator group — that ingests CPAT and health-team outputs as inputs and produces a single coherent assessment. It does not generate new estimates where existing tools already do. It harmonises, presents, and benchmarks. The discipline is its main contribution: a single value of statistical life, a single carbon shadow price, a single set of accident-cost parameters, applied consistently across all the sectoral inputs in a single country.

## Key questions and the climate–health join

Part B is where most of the diagnostic’s key questions live, because it is the part that asks the system-level question Part A cannot reach. The questions below are grouped to mirror the seven-section spine and the climate–health capacities the two World Bank programs already hold. Many are answered by harmonising existing outputs rather than by new computation — the point of the synthesis layer.

### Benchmarking: consumption, tax levels and gaps

*The climate and health programs each benchmark consumption and tax levels in their own domain. The diagnostic asks whether they can be benchmarked together, on a common externality footing.*

1.  **Joint tax benchmarking.** Can a single assessment benchmark how all countries tax goods with externalities — fuels, tobacco, alcohol and sugar-sweetened beverages — on one comparable basis? The climate program’s Total Carbon Price expresses how a country taxes carbon across fuel products; the health program calculates how tobacco, alcohol and SSBs are taxed.

2.  **Tax per unit of harmful content.** Just as the Total Carbon Price expresses fuel taxes per unit of carbon content, can alcohol excises be expressed per unit of pure alcohol content — revealing, as for fuels, where a country taxes different products of the same class inconsistently?

3.  **Share of price from excise.** What share of the consumer price of each taxed good comes from excise? The health program calculates this for health-related products; the climate program holds the data for fuels but does not yet report it.

4.  **Tax gaps against social cost.** How do current excises compare with the social costs of the taxed goods? The climate program compares fuel excises with fuel social costs directly. Does the health program compare current tobacco, alcohol and SSB excises with the social costs of those products, beyond citing the total cost of tobacco use?

5.  **Consumption composition.** How has consumption evolved — in aggregate and by subcategory of fuel and of alcohol — and how is it split across households today?

### Disease burden and affordability

6.  **Baseline disease burden.** What are the baseline fatalities and DALYs attributable to the taxed goods — from air pollution linked to fuel consumption, and from tobacco and alcohol consumption — and how do they link back to the quantities the tax system can move?

7.  **Affordability over time.** How has the excise-inclusive price of each taxed good moved relative to CPI inflation and to household incomes? The health program tracks this for health products; the climate program holds but does not report the equivalent for fuels.

### Reform analysis: revenue, prices, use, disease and equity

*Both programs already quantify the first-order effects of tax reform. The diagnostic’s reform questions ask them in one place and on one valuation spine.*

8.  **Revenue.** How much revenue would a given reform raise? Both programs quantify this in their domains.

9.  **Prices.** How would the reform change product prices? Both programs quantify pass-through.

10. **Product use.** By how much would the reform reduce consumption — of fuels (climate program) and of health-related products (health program)?

11. **Disease averted.** How many fatalities and DALYs would the reform avert, and what health-care costs would it avoid? The climate program estimates this for air pollution; the health program for tobacco and alcohol.

12. **Equity.** How are the welfare effects distributed across income groups, and how does revenue recycling change the picture? The climate program quantifies fuel-price incidence for some 125 countries using household surveys and input-output tables; tobacco incidence is simulated country-by-country (e.g. with the TOBACTAX tool). Can the household surveys already used in CPAT be reopened to simulate the equity effects of health taxes — feasible for tobacco and alcohol, though SSBs may not be separable in survey data?

13. **Macroeconomic effects.** What are the output and employment effects of health-related taxes? The health program does not yet estimate these, but the revenue figures it produces would support a fiscal-multiplier analysis of the kind the climate program runs.

14. **Informality and illicit trade.** How vulnerable is each tax to evasion relative to conventional taxes? The climate program argues fuel taxes are harder to evade than income tax or VAT; the health program treats illicit trade as a risk for health taxes. Both cases are strengthened by comparing that vulnerability with the vulnerability of the taxes the excise would substitute for.

### Design: specific versus ad valorem

15. **Rate structure.** Should the externality-correcting component be levied as a specific rate rather than ad valorem? Both programs advise specific rates for externalities.

16. **Indexation.** How should specific rates be indexed so that real value is not eroded between Finance Acts? Both programs recommend inflation updating — the structural fix Part A surfaces from the erosion-and-restoration cycle.

## Proposed report structure

We propose a fixed report structure with seven sections. It is the same in both tiers; the difference is depth and data requirements, not architecture. The discipline of fixed structure matters: it allows a country team to produce the report without negotiating its scope each time, allows comparison across countries, and allows incremental improvement of any single section without disturbing the rest.

### 

  -----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  **Section**   **Title**                       **Purpose**
  ------------- ------------------------------- -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  **1**         Tax baseline and revenue        What rates apply now, what they yield, who pays. Explicit and implicit subsidies. Effective per-litre and per-tCO2 rates after VAT and cascading.

  **2**         Externality estimates           Carbon, local air pollution, accidents, congestion, road damage. Per litre and per vkm where relevant. Drawn from CPAT, health-team outputs, IMF GEPR, country sources.

  **3**         Optimal corrective rate         Naive Pigouvian sum and second-best rate adjusted for mileage versus fuel-economy elasticity decomposition. Sensitivity ranges across SCC, VSL and elasticities.

  **4**         Gap analysis                    Current versus optimal, by fuel. Decomposition of the gap by externality category. Which gaps are best closed by fuel tax versus dedicated instruments.

  **5**         Distributional incidence        Welfare effects across deciles, urban versus rural, formal versus informal transport. Drawn directly from CPAT incidence module where available.

  **6**         International norm comparator   Statutory rates versus regional and OECD benchmarks. Effective carbon rate versus TECP comparator group. CBAM and border-adjustment exposure.

  **7**         Reform pathway                  Sequenced instrument package, revenue projection, recycling options, compensation design, implementation calendar. Practical, not theoretical.
  -----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Sub-question added to Section 2.** Building on the original FVTD design, Part B as deployed here adds a ranking sub-question to Section 2: what is the biggest externality not currently priced by the tax system? The ranking is read off the Section 2 component table — the largest gap between estimated externality and current effective rate, by fuel — and used to prioritise the Section 7 reform pathway. The sub-question is what makes Part B feed cleanly into Part C.

### Tier 1 (capable LMICs and UMICs)

Tier 1 uses country-specific data where available. Country VSL is computed by income-elasticity transfer from an OECD baseline rather than borrowed wholesale. Country-specific elasticities are used where credible estimates exist; pooled regional estimates are used otherwise, with sensitivity ranges. Active-travel health benefits are quantified using the WHO HEAT methodology. Distinct urban and rural externality profiles are presented separately. Vehicle-stock vintage modelling is included in Section 7 to address Gruenspecht effects on purchase taxes.

Candidate countries: Chile, Colombia, South Africa, Mexico, Brazil, Turkey, Indonesia, Philippines, Thailand. Egypt and Vietnam are borderline.

### Tier 2 (LICs and weak-data LMICs)

Tier 2 uses the same seven-section spine but with simplified methods. Benefit-transferred VSL is used with explicit caveats. Pooled regional elasticities are used throughout. Externalities are estimated via population-weighted exposure times emission factor times concentration-response, without dispersion modelling. Congestion is computed only for the primary city and assumed negligible elsewhere. Active-travel benefits are noted qualitatively only. The second-best optimisation is dropped; a naive Pigouvian rate with a sensitivity corridor is reported instead.

The deliverable is direction and magnitude rather than a precise optimal rate. “Diesel is undertaxed by approximately X to Y dollars per litre” is more useful than a false-precision point estimate.

Candidate countries: most of the IDA caseload — Uganda, Tanzania, Rwanda, Ethiopia, Mozambique, Ghana, Senegal, Kenya at the upper end. Pakistan and Bangladesh fit Tier 2 despite being LMICs.

## What the join does and does not require

Two scoping points keep the joint offering tractable. First, the equity apparatus need not be fully unified. CPAT models the indirect consumption of fuels used as inputs to other goods, which is why it harmonises household surveys with input-output tables. Health taxes need no such treatment: alcohol, tobacco and SSBs are consumed directly, not used as inputs to producing other goods, and health excises are levied downstream on end products. So the household-survey apparatus can be reused for health-tax incidence without reconciling it against input-output tables.

Second, the join is also an opportunity to consolidate tooling. A shared inventory of the analytical tools held by both teams could be surfaced on the excise-tax section of the relevant website, and the diagnostic’s outputs could feed a joint visualisation — a Power BI dashboard or a PFR visualisation-tool input — so that country teams reach one place for both climate and health excise analysis.

**Open implementation questions.** Three items remain to be settled as the joint offering is built:

- Identify the full list of analytical tools held by both the climate and health teams and surface them on the excise-tax section of the website.

- Decide whether a joint Power BI website is feasible, or whether the outputs are better delivered as an input to the PFR visualisation tool.

- Confirm which household surveys can be reopened for health-tax equity analysis, and for which products the incidence is separately identifiable.

# B2. Existing international work

Four bodies of international work form the analytical foundation.

### B2.1 The IMF Getting Energy Prices Right framework

Parry, Heine, Li and Lis (2014) developed the most influential cross-country framework for assessing externality-corrective fuel taxes. Its operational form is the corrective fuel tax equals carbon damages plus local air pollution damages plus congestion plus accidents plus road damage, with each term measured per litre of fuel and adjusted for the share of behavioural response on the mileage versus fuel-economy margin. The IMF publishes country estimates regularly, most recently in the Black-Parry-Vernon-Zhunussova fossil-fuel subsidy updates. The framework is the single most useful global benchmark.

Strengths: full country coverage, transparent methodology, regular updates, integrated with the IMF implicit-subsidy concept. Weaknesses: necessarily uses pooled or extrapolated parameters in countries with thin local data; the headline corrective-tax number masks substantial uncertainty; not designed as a country-engagement document but as a global comparative exercise.

### B2.2 The CE Delft Handbook on External Costs of Transport

The European Commission Handbook on External Costs of Transport, originally produced in 2008 by CE Delft and updated in 2019, is the most detailed methodological reference in existence. It covers all transport modes; provides recommended values for VSL, accidents, air pollution, climate, noise, congestion and infrastructure costs; and gives explicit guidance on value-transfer to non-EU contexts. EU member states reference it in national appraisal frameworks.

Strengths: rigour, comprehensiveness, regular updates, official endorsement. Weaknesses: calibrated for European conditions; the value-transfer guidance to LICs is light; not aimed at fuel-tax assessment specifically.

### B2.3 OECD Effective Carbon Rates and Taxing Energy Use

The OECD Taxing Energy Use series and the Effective Carbon Rate metric provide standardised cross-country measurement of explicit and implicit carbon prices on fuels. The methodology is transparent and the series is regularly updated. The OECD Carbon Pricing Score is a normative yardstick benchmarking countries against an EUR 60 per tonne reference.

Strengths: comparable carbon-rate measurement across about eighty countries, transparent methodology. Weaknesses: scope is limited to the carbon dimension; does not cover the other externalities.

### B2.4 Parry-Strand and the country-application templates

Parry and Strand (2012) applied the IMF framework explicitly as a transferable template, with Chile as the worked example. The same template was applied by Anton-Sarabia and Hernandez-Trillo to Mexico and by Heine and colleagues to Brazil. The Bijgaart, Klenert and Mattauch extension adds active-travel health benefits, increasing optimal fuel taxes by 38 to 44 per cent in UK and US applications.

These applications are the closest published analogues to what the FVTD would produce. They are academic studies, not institutional products, but they demonstrate that the methodology can be applied to country conditions with reasonable data.

# B3. Existing national work

National practice is more uneven than international practice. The UK is the most institutionalised case for valuation discipline. Other countries do parts of the work but rarely the whole.

### B3.1 The United Kingdom

The UK is the cleanest example of standardised valuation parameters. The Treasury Green Book sets the framework for cost-benefit analysis across government. The Department for Transport TAG (Transport Analysis Guidance, formerly WebTAG) provides values for VSL via willingness-to-pay surveys, time savings, accident costs by casualty type, and noise. The Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs publishes damage-cost estimates per tonne for PM2.5, NOx, SO2 and ammonia. The Department for Energy Security and Net Zero publishes a carbon-values trajectory used in all government appraisal.

These are updated annually or near-annually. They are mandatory for regulatory impact assessment. The result is a rare situation in which a transport modeller, an air-pollution analyst, and a climate analyst working on the same project use the same VSL and the same carbon price by default.

The UK does not produce a recurring fuel-tax diagnostic of the kind we propose. Fuel duty rates are set in the Budget on revenue and political grounds. But the valuation discipline is exemplary and is what we propose to borrow.

### B3.2 Chile

Chile has the strongest LMIC analytical foundation. The Parry-Strand application produced a full externality-corrective tax assessment. Chile introduced a carbon component on stationary sources in 2014 and has continued to develop environmental tax architecture. The Ministry of Environment maintains air-pollution exposure data of reasonable quality. There is no recurring institutional diagnostic, but most of the underlying analytical infrastructure is in place.

### B3.3 Colombia

Colombia has done strong work in the component pieces but has not integrated them. DNP and the Ministry of Environment have produced PM2.5 mortality valuations — the 2018 estimate placed annual mortality cost at about 1.2 per cent of GDP. Colombia has had a national carbon tax since 2017 and has a carbon-credit offset mechanism. Bogota emissions inventories are technically strong. What is missing is the synthesis layer joining tax design to externality valuation.

### B3.4 Brazil and Mexico

Both have academic optimal-fuel-tax computations applied to their conditions. Mexico has had a carbon component on fuels since 2014. Brazil's distinctive ethanol question is treated in Heine et al.: the largest externality for gasoline and ethanol is accidents, while air pollution dominates for diesel. Neither country institutionalises the analysis.

### B3.5 South Africa

South Africa has the most developed legislative carbon-pricing architecture among middle-income countries, with a carbon tax operating since 2019, fuel-levy escalators, and Treasury budget reviews that engage with externality reasoning. The integrated diagnostic is still missing.

### B3.6 Sub-Saharan Africa more broadly

The Institute for Fiscal Studies has produced what is in effect the closest existing template for an LIC-applicable diagnostic: its report on green motor taxation in sub-Saharan Africa, funded by the FCDO and the Gates Foundation, walks through the four main externalities for SSA conditions, documents fuel and vehicle tax structures across Ethiopia, Ghana, Rwanda and Uganda, and uses microsimulation on household survey data to compute incidence. It is calibrated for LIC realities — very low motorisation, high pedestrian-fatality share, geographic concentration of vehicles in capitals.

It is an academic study, not a government product. But it is the analytical template a Tier-2 diagnostic should follow.

### B3.7 What national practice tells us

Three points emerge. First, no country produces, as a recurring institutional output, the integrated diagnostic we are proposing. The gap is real. Second, the UK discipline of standardised valuation parameters is the model worth copying — not the specific values, which are UK-specific, but the institutional habit of having one VSL, one carbon price, one set of pollution damage costs that all government analysts use. Third, the methodology to do the work in developing-country settings already exists; what is missing is the synthesis.

# B4. Data needs and gaps

The realistic question is not whether the diagnostic can be done but how much country-specific data is needed for the answer to be defensible. The table below lists the inputs by section, distinguishes between Tier 1 and Tier 2 requirements, and flags where each input typically comes from.

  **Implicit subsidies**                     IMF Black-Parry-Vernon updates                                               Same                                                                   Low. Standardised globally.

  **Accident costs**                         Police data, Health Ministry, WHO road safety                                WHO Global Status Report on Road Safety                                High. Accident reporting is poor in most LICs and underestimates pedestrian deaths.

  **Congestion**                             City speed-flow data, TomTom or local                                        Skip outside primary city; primary city via comparator extrapolation   High. Real data is rare; comparator extrapolation has wide error bars.
