### B4.1 The three serious gaps

Three data gaps will dominate practical use of the diagnostic in developing-country settings.

- **Local air pollution exposure.** GBD provides country-level mortality estimates that are usable, but the spatial granularity needed to attribute mortality to transport-sector emissions specifically is missing in most LICs and many LMICs. The Climate and Health Program is investing in this, but the gap will persist. The diagnostic should report explicit ranges rather than point estimates and flag when the underlying exposure data is GBD-default rather than country-specific.

- **Accident cost estimation.** Police accident reporting is incomplete in most developing countries and systematically undercounts pedestrian and cyclist fatalities — exactly the categories most relevant for assessing the external accident cost of motorised travel. The WHO Global Status Report on Road Safety provides corrected estimates but at country level only. For Tier 1 work the diagnostic should triangulate police, health-ministry mortuary, and WHO-corrected estimates and report the range.

- **Local fuel-price elasticities.** Almost no LIC has a credible local estimate. Pooled regional or global elasticities must be used, with sensitivity analysis. The corrective fuel tax can vary by 20 to 30 per cent across plausible elasticity ranges, so this is a material uncertainty that the report must surface, not bury.

### B4.2 What the diagnostic does not require

To keep the diagnostic tractable, several things are deliberately out of scope. New modelling capacity is not required — CPAT and Climate and Health Program outputs are inputs, not things the diagnostic re-runs. Country-specific concentration-response functions are not required — pooled functions from GBD are used. Bottom-up emissions inventories are not required — fuel-consumption-based estimates are sufficient. Detailed urban transport modelling is not required — congestion is treated as a single externality term per litre with explicit uncertainty.

The principle is to use the best existing input wherever possible and to be honest about ranges where it does not exist. The diagnostic value is in synthesis and discipline, not in new computation.

# B5. The valuation spine: standardized parameters

Following the UK example, the diagnostic uses a fixed set of valuation parameters across all sections of any single country report. The parameters are not country-specific — that is precisely the point. Country-specific data enters via the externality estimates themselves (exposure, accident counts, fuel volumes), but the values applied to those quantities are drawn from a standard table. This avoids the problem of one analyst using a 2020 SCC and another a 2030 SCC in the same report.

### B5.1 Recommended defaults

  ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  **Parameter**                              **Default value**                                                    **Source / sensitivity range**
  ------------------------------------------ -------------------------------------------------------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  **Carbon shadow price**                    USD 75/tCO2 (2026), rising 2 per cent annually                       WB-IMF carbon price floor for high-income countries; sensitivity USD 50–150.

  **VSL — high-income baseline**             USD 4.7 million (OECD 2024)                                          OECD Mortality Risk Valuation. Sensitivity +/- 30 per cent.

  **VSL income elasticity for transfer**     1.0                                                                  OECD recommendation. Sensitivity 0.8–1.2.

  **PM2.5 damage cost**                      Country-specific from VSL × mortality CRF                            Computed, not assumed. CRF from GBD or country if available.

  **Fuel-price elasticity**                  −0.3 short run, −0.6 long run                                        Pooled estimates from Sterner and others. Sensitivity −0.2 to −0.8.

  **Mileage share of fuel-price response**   0.5                                                                  IMF GEPR default. Sensitivity 0.35–0.65.

  **Discount rate**                          Country social discount rate where published, otherwise 5 per cent   Sensitivity 3–7 per cent.
  ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

These defaults are placeholders for discussion. The substantive point is that they should be set once for the diagnostic product, applied across all country reports, and updated annually. Country teams can deviate with explicit justification, but the default applies otherwise.

# B6. Worked example: a draft Tier 2 report

The remainder of this section illustrates what a complete Tier 2 report would look like, using a stylised East African LIC for concreteness. The country is fictitious but the parameters are realistic. The example is meant to show the shape and length of the deliverable rather than to make claims about any actual country. A real report would substitute country-specific data and reference its sources explicitly.

The example below covers the seven-section spine. Tier 1 reports would run thirty to forty pages with the same architecture; the additional length comes from country-specific elasticities, vintage modelling, and an active-travel benefits sub-section.

### B6.1 Section 1 — Tax baseline and revenue

Country X levies a specific excise of USD 0.18 per litre on gasoline and USD 0.10 per litre on diesel, plus a road-maintenance levy of USD 0.05 per litre on both fuels and a value-added tax of 18 per cent applied to the post-excise price. Kerosene is untaxed and partially subsidised through wholesale-price intervention. Liquefied petroleum gas is zero-rated for VAT. Vehicle taxes consist of import duty (25 per cent for new passenger vehicles, 35 per cent for vehicles older than eight years), an annual circulation fee of USD 30 to USD 200 by engine size, and a one-time first-registration fee.

Total fuel-related tax revenue was approximately USD 320 million in 2024, equivalent to 1.4 per cent of GDP and 7 per cent of total tax revenue. Vehicle-related taxes raised an additional USD 95 million.

Implicit subsidies, computed using the IMF post-tax methodology and a USD 75 per tonne carbon price, amount to USD 410 million annually — that is, the undercharging of external costs exceeds direct fuel-tax revenue. The largest implicit-subsidy components are local air pollution (43 per cent of the total) and accidents (31 per cent).

### B6.2 Section 2 — Externality estimates

#### Carbon

Gasoline combustion emits approximately 2.3 kgCO2 per litre; diesel emits 2.7 kgCO2 per litre. At a USD 75 per tonne carbon shadow price, the carbon externality is USD 0.17 per litre of gasoline and USD 0.20 per litre of diesel. Sensitivity range across USD 50 to USD 150 per tonne is USD 0.12 to USD 0.35 per litre.

#### Local air pollution

Climate and Health Program estimates attribute approximately 8,400 premature deaths annually to ambient PM2.5 in Country X, of which transport sources contribute an estimated 28 per cent. At an income-transferred VSL of USD 0.45 million (computed from the OECD baseline of USD 4.7 million and Country X GNI per capita using a transfer elasticity of 1.0), the transport-attributable PM2.5 mortality cost is approximately USD 1,060 million annually.

Allocated across diesel and gasoline consumption by emission factor and fuel volume, this implies USD 0.42 per litre of diesel and USD 0.09 per litre of gasoline. The diesel figure is large because diesel emits substantially more PM2.5 per litre than gasoline and is concentrated in urban areas. Sensitivity range, accounting for VSL and CRF uncertainty, is USD 0.25 to USD 0.65 per litre of diesel.

#### Accidents

WHO Global Status Report estimates road-traffic mortality in Country X at 27 deaths per 100,000 population, with pedestrians accounting for 47 per cent of fatalities. Annual road deaths are approximately 14,000. Total external accident cost — applying VSL and a morbidity multiplier of 1.5 — is approximately USD 9.5 billion.

Allocated to per-litre fuel cost using the standard methodology, the accident externality is approximately USD 0.28 per litre of gasoline and USD 0.31 per litre of diesel. The high pedestrian-fatality share, characteristic of LICs, makes accident externalities a larger component of the total than in OECD applications. Sensitivity range is USD 0.18 to USD 0.45 per litre.

#### Congestion

Estimated for the primary city only. Comparator-based extrapolation from Nairobi and Addis Ababa suggests an average congestion externality of USD 0.08 per litre of fuel consumed in the capital, weighted by the capital share of national fuel consumption (approximately 35 per cent). The national-average congestion externality is therefore USD 0.03 per litre. This is a low-confidence estimate and should be reported as such.

#### Road damage

Concentrated in heavy goods vehicles. Estimated at USD 0.04 per litre of diesel and negligible for gasoline.

#### The biggest externality not currently priced

For Country X, the answer is local air pollution from diesel: approximately USD 0.42 per litre against a current effective rate that does not reflect it. The accident externality on both fuels is the second-largest gap. The carbon externality is third, despite being the dimension most frequently discussed in public debate. This ranking matters for Part C: it identifies where the reform pathway should focus first.

### B6.3 Section 3 — Optimal corrective rate

Summing the externality components yields a naive Pigouvian rate of approximately USD 0.57 per litre of gasoline and USD 0.97 per litre of diesel. Adjusting for the mileage-share elasticity decomposition (default 0.5) gives second-best corrective rates of approximately USD 0.39 per litre of gasoline and USD 0.65 per litre of diesel.

  -----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  **Component (USD / litre)**   **Gasoline central**   **Gasoline range**   **Diesel central**   **Diesel range**
  ----------------------------- ---------------------- -------------------- -------------------- ------------------
  **Carbon**                    0.17                   0.12–0.35            0.20                 0.14–0.41

  **Air pollution**             0.09                   0.05–0.14            0.42                 0.25–0.65

  **Accidents**                 0.28                   0.18–0.45            0.31                 0.20–0.50

  **Congestion**                0.03                   0.01–0.06            0.03                 0.01–0.06

  **Road damage**               0.00                   0.00–0.01            0.04                 0.02–0.06

  **Naive sum**                 0.57                   0.36–1.01            0.97                 0.62–1.68

  **Second-best**               0.39                   0.25–0.70            0.65                 0.42–1.15
  -----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

### B6.4 Section 4 — Gap analysis

Current effective rates are USD 0.23 per litre on gasoline and USD 0.15 per litre on diesel. Gaps versus the second-best corrective rate are USD 0.16 per litre for gasoline and USD 0.50 per litre for diesel. Diesel is the much larger problem, driven primarily by air pollution and accidents.

This is a familiar pattern in developing-country settings: gasoline is roughly correctly taxed; diesel is substantially undertaxed. The gap is not a curiosity but a direct fiscal-and-health argument for diesel-tax reform.

Closing the gap on diesel by USD 0.50 per litre would raise approximately USD 230 million annually — increasing total fuel-tax revenue by 70 per cent and approaching 1 per cent of GDP. The implicit-subsidy welfare gain would be larger still, since avoided health and accident costs accrue independently of revenue.

### B6.5 Section 5 — Distributional incidence

CPAT incidence analysis (drawing on Country X 2019 Household Budget Survey) shows that direct fuel-tax incidence is mildly progressive on gasoline (richer households spend a higher share of total expenditure on private motoring) and approximately neutral on diesel (heavily mediated through public transport fares and goods prices). The combined incidence of a USD 0.50 per litre diesel-tax increase, before recycling, is regressive by 0.7 percentage points of expenditure between the bottom and top quintile.

Three of four standard recycling options reverse the regressivity: a flat per-household transfer financed by 30 per cent of the new revenue produces a net-progressive package; a doubled targeted social-protection transfer to bottom-quintile households produces a strongly progressive package; reductions in payroll tax produce a roughly distribution-neutral package; reductions in VAT produce a marginally regressive package.

### B6.6 Section 6 — International norm comparator

Country X effective fuel tax rates are below the East African Community average and well below sub-Saharan African LMIC averages. The OECD effective carbon rate on gasoline (USD 74 per tonne) and diesel (USD 56 per tonne) place Country X in the bottom quartile globally. CBAM exposure is currently low because Country X exports are largely agricultural; this will change if cement or fertiliser exports expand.

Comparable LICs that have raised diesel tax over the past decade (Rwanda, Ghana, Kenya in steps) have done so without the macroeconomic disruption commonly feared, particularly when reform was sequenced with targeted social protection. Country X has more fiscal space for reform than the political debate currently assumes.

### B6.7 Section 7 — Reform pathway (handed to Part C)

In a standalone FVTD report, Section 7 would conclude with a sequenced reform package. In the combined three-part diagnostic, Section 7 is migrated upward into Part C, where it is integrated with the Part A reform candidates, comparator-country experience, and political-economy analysis. A summary appears here for completeness; the full pathway is set out in Part C.

- **Year 1:** USD 0.15 per litre diesel excise increase. Revenue use: 30 per cent into a flat per-household transfer through existing social-protection channels; 70 per cent to general revenue. Communications campaign emphasising the health and road-safety justification, not the climate justification, which polls poorly in Country X.

- **Year 2:** Further USD 0.15 per litre diesel increase. Convert the per-household transfer into a permanent indexed component of the social safety net. Introduce a feebate on imported vehicles based on emissions and weight to begin addressing fleet composition without a Gruenspecht effect.

- **Year 3:** Final USD 0.20 per litre diesel increase, closing roughly two-thirds of the original gap. Begin scoping a distance-based heavy-goods-vehicle charge to address the road-damage and accident externalities that fuel tax addresses imperfectly. Update the diagnostic at this point with new exposure and accident data.

The package raises an estimated additional USD 230 million in annual revenue at full implementation, leaves the bottom quintile better off in net terms, and approximately halves the implicit-subsidy gap. It does not close the gap entirely; full closure would require complementary instruments beyond fuel taxation.

**\**

**PART C**

**Policy Pathways**

*Existing proposals, success stories, narrative political-economy analysis, and a sequenced reform package*

# C1. Purpose and structure

Parts A and B both produce lists of policy candidates. Part A reads them off the schedule — erosion patterns, gaps relative to peer countries, structural anomalies, rate inversions. Part B reads them off the externality estimates — the largest gap between damage and current effective rate, by fuel and by externality category. Neither part sequences candidates, references comparator experience, or accounts for political tractability. Part C does.

Part C draws on five inputs: (i) the structural anomalies, gaps and erosion patterns surfaced by Part A; (ii) the externality-gap and incidence findings from Part B; (iii) international benchmarks and IMF Getting Energy Prices Right comparators; (iv) comparator-country success stories; and (v) a narrative political-economy analysis. The substantive findings of Parts A and B are not repeated here. Where Part C refers to a finding it does so by reference; the underlying analysis lives in the relevant earlier section.

The remainder of this Part is organised in five sections.

- C2 — Existing proposals. The IMF baseline benchmarks and a structured summary of the Part A and Part B reform candidates.

- C3 — Success stories. Comparator countries that have sequenced similar reforms without macroeconomic disruption.

- C4 — Narrative political-economy analysis. Which reforms are politically tractable in which conditions, why, and with what compensation design.

- C5 — A sequenced reform pathway. A three-year package combining Part A and Part B candidates, ordered by tractability and yield.

- C6 — Conclusion.

## Key questions Part C answers

*Part C converts the findings of Parts A and B into a reform calendar. Its key questions are about sequencing, tractability and compensation — not about new substantive findings.*

17. **Sequencing.** Given the candidate reforms from Parts A and B, which comes first, and what is the right ordering by political tractability, fiscal yield and administrative readiness?

18. **Tractability.** Which reforms can survive contact with politics in this country — reading the winners and losers directly off the schedule structure and the externality decomposition?

19. **Compensation.** How should revenue be recycled so that the bottom of the distribution is protected, and is the compensation announced simultaneously with the reform rather than afterwards?

20. **Framing.** Should the reform be argued on health and road-safety grounds or on climate grounds, given that air pollution and accidents dominate the externality gap in most LICs?

21. **Comparators.** Which comparator-country experiences — drawn from peers the policy audience considers similar — give the proposal political weight?

# C2. Existing proposals and the candidates inherited from Parts A and B

### C2.1 The IMF Getting Energy Prices Right baseline

The IMF GEPR framework remains the most useful global comparator for fuel and vehicle taxation. Its operational form — the corrective fuel tax equals carbon damages plus local air pollution damages plus congestion plus accidents plus road damage — is the same framework Part B's Section 2 operates within. The IMF publishes country estimates regularly through the Black-Parry-Vernon-Zhunussova fossil-fuel subsidy updates. For any country running the combined diagnostic, the IMF GEPR numbers are the natural cross-check against the Part B point estimates: where they agree, the case for reform is strengthened; where they disagree, the divergence itself becomes a topic of country dialogue.

The IMF's normative recommendation is convergence toward an internalised corrective rate. The diagnostic does not impose this normative position. It presents the gap and the comparator and lets the country team decide how much of the gap to close in what timeframe.

### C2.2 The Part A reform candidates

Part A surfaced three reform candidates from the schedule itself, plus a structural reform (indexation) and a category-broadening candidate (sugar-graduated SSB). They are restated here in summary form.

  -----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  **Candidate**                                                                   **What it would do**
  ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  **Redenominate the Sierra Leonean wine schedule**                               FA2024 rates in Old Leones translate to essentially zero excise after the 2022 1,000:1 redenomination. A one-line schedule amendment in the next Finance Act would restore the intended rates. Negligible fiscal yield but a transparency win.

  **Lift Sierra Leonean cigarette excise toward Uganda's lowest tier**            Sierra Leone runs at approximately USD 0.14 per pack against Uganda's USD 0.35 to 1.07. A phased path of three Finance Acts at plus 30 per cent each would bring the rate toward Uganda's lowest tier. The base is small (low smoking prevalence) so the fiscal yield is modest; the public-health case is well-evidenced.

  **Introduce sugar-content-graduated SSB excise in both countries**              Uganda taxes all non-alcoholic beverages including juice at a flat 12 per cent or UGX 250 per litre; Sierra Leone taxes only energy drinks and imported juice. UK SDIL and South Africa HPL demonstrate the design can be implemented. The rate gap to peers is largest here and the public-health rationale is well-evidenced.

  **Index specific rates to inflation**                                           Both countries' specific rates show clear erosion-and-restoration cycles. Indexation removes the political cost of restoration without losing real revenue. Standard reform with a long track record in OECD countries.

  **Carbon-tax overlay on fuel, or graduated emissions-based vehicle taxation**   Currently fuel excise does environmental work only by accident — Uganda's UGX 1,550 per litre on petrol corresponds to an implicit carbon rate that varies with international fuel prices. An explicit carbon component would make this visible. Part B picks this up directly.
  -----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

### C2.3 The Part B reform candidates

Part B's Section 7 sketch for Country X produced four candidates that generalise across most Tier 2 settings. They are restated here without re-derivation.

  --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  **Candidate**                                           **What it would do**
  ------------------------------------------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  **Phased diesel-tax closure of the externality gap**    In Country X, USD 0.50 per litre over three years closes roughly two-thirds of the gap to the second-best corrective rate. Air pollution and accidents drive the gap; the case is health-and-safety, not climate. Revenue: approximately 1 per cent of GDP at full implementation.

  **Recycling design: per-household transfer**            30 per cent of new revenue into a flat per-household transfer through existing social-protection channels neutralises the regressivity of the diesel-tax increase. The bottom quintile is better off in net terms. In year two, the transfer is institutionalised as a permanent indexed component of the social safety net.

  **Emissions-and-weight feebate on imported vehicles**   Begins addressing fleet composition without a Gruenspecht effect (i.e. without locking in old vehicles by raising the price of new ones). Year-two reform.

  **Distance-based heavy-goods-vehicle charge**           Addresses the road-damage and accident externalities that fuel tax addresses imperfectly. Year-three reform; requires administrative infrastructure that takes time to build.
  --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Read together, the candidates from Parts A and B cover three reform domains: rate-level reforms (cigarette and SSB convergence, diesel-tax closure); structural reforms (indexation, recycling design, feebate, distance-based charge); and transparency reforms (wine redenomination). The sequencing of these candidates is what Part C contributes.

# C3. Success stories — comparator-country experience

Reform proposals carry more political weight when grounded in comparable experience. Country teams need to be able to say “this is what Ghana did, this is what Rwanda did, this is what worked, this is what didn't”. The following are short comparator vignettes drawn from public-domain sources and from the existing FVTD national-practice review (Part B section B3).

### C3.1 Rwanda, Ghana and Kenya — phased diesel-tax increases

All three countries have raised diesel tax over the past decade in steps. None has experienced the macroeconomic disruption commonly feared in advance of such reforms. Three features are common to the successful sequencing: (i) increases were announced in advance and bundled across the fuel slate (petrol and diesel together, with diesel rising faster) so that no single fuel-using sector was singled out; (ii) increases were sequenced with targeted social protection — Rwanda's Vision Umurenge Programme, Ghana's LEAP, Kenya's Inua Jamii — so that bottom-quintile households were visibly compensated; (iii) the public communication emphasised the health and road-safety justification rather than the climate justification. The diesel case is health-and-safety, not climate; LIC publics respond to it differently.

The implication for the diagnostic: comparator references should be drawn from countries the policy audience considers similar, not from OECD precedents. A Ugandan Permanent Secretary will respond more strongly to “Rwanda did this” than to “Denmark did this”, even where the Danish case is methodologically more rigorous.

### C3.2 South Africa — legislative carbon-pricing architecture

South Africa has the most developed legislative carbon-pricing architecture among middle-income countries. The carbon tax operating since 2019 covers approximately 80 per cent of national emissions. Fuel-levy escalators are a regular feature of the annual Budget Review. Treasury budget reviews engage with externality reasoning more explicitly than is typical at this income level. Two features of the South African design are worth replicating: (i) the carbon component is layered on existing fuel levies rather than imposed alongside them, which simplifies administration; (ii) the headline rate is announced with a multi-year trajectory rather than year by year, which reduces the political cost of each annual increase.

The constraint on direct replication is administrative capacity. South Africa has stronger revenue and tax administration than most lower-income comparators. A Tier 2 application of the South African design would need to simplify.

### C3.3 Mexico, Chile, Colombia — carbon components on fuels

Mexico introduced a carbon component on fuels in 2014. Chile introduced a carbon component on stationary sources in 2014 and has continued to develop environmental tax architecture. Colombia has had a national carbon tax since 2017 with a carbon-credit offset mechanism. In each case the headline rate is modest by OECD standards but the institutional precedent matters: a country that already has “a carbon tax on fuels”, even at a low rate, can raise it through ordinary budget processes; a country introducing one from scratch faces a much steeper political hurdle. Phasing-in matters more than the level.

### C3.4 The UK — valuation discipline

The UK does not produce a recurring fuel-tax diagnostic of the kind proposed here, but it does institutionalise the valuation discipline that Part B borrows. A single VSL, a single carbon trajectory, a single set of pollution damage costs are used across government appraisal. The implication for the diagnostic is not to copy the UK numbers but to copy the institutional habit: set the parameters once, apply them everywhere in a country report, update annually.

### C3.5 What does not work — anti-patterns from comparator experience

The literature on failed fuel-subsidy reform is large and consistent. Three anti-patterns appear repeatedly.

- **Reform announced without recycling design.** Ecuador 2019, Indonesia 2022, Iran 2019, Nigeria multiple times. A subsidy cut or fuel-tax increase is announced; affected populations protest; the reform is reversed or watered down. The Part B recycling design — a flat per-household transfer financed by a fraction of the new revenue — is the most reliable counterweight, but only if it is announced simultaneously with the reform, not afterwards.

- **Reform sold on climate grounds in LICs.** Climate justification polls poorly in countries where most fuel-buyers will not personally experience the worst consequences of global warming. The health and road-safety justification polls substantially better and is empirically the larger component of the externality gap in LICs. The communications choice is not a betrayal of the climate logic; it is a recognition that the local pollution and accident gains are larger in absolute terms.

- **Reform on a single instrument.** Raising fuel excise without addressing vehicle taxation produces a known failure mode: high-emission vehicles continue to enter the fleet and lock in the future fuel-use base. The Part B Year 2 feebate addresses this directly. Reform pathways need to address the stock as well as the flow.

# C4. Narrative political-economy analysis

Reform proposals that survive contact with politics share recognisable features. This section reads political-economy dynamics directly off the schedules diagnosed in Part A and the externality estimates in Part B. The objective is not to produce a general theory but to give country teams a structured way of thinking about which reforms are tractable in which conditions.

### C4.1 Who wins and who loses from the status quo

Every excise line creates winners and losers. Reform that re-allocates these gains and losses creates active political opposition. The first step in any political-economy analysis is to map them.

On the producer side, local-content discounts in the alcohol regimes of both Uganda and Sierra Leone create politically organised winners. Uganda's beer regime gives a 50 per cent rate discount to producers using at least 75 per cent local raw material; Sierra Leone's four-band local-content system (D1–D4) graduates the rate by share of local input. These bands look like industrial policy. From a political-economy perspective they are also producer protection: domestic agricultural input suppliers, domestic brewers, and the politicians representing their constituencies. Reform that flattens the bands or raises the discounted rate confronts a recognisable lobby. The diagnostic should not assume away that constraint.

On the consumer side, fuel-tax increases are spatially concentrated. Urban motorists pay more directly; informal-sector transport workers (matatu and boda boda drivers in East Africa, poda poda drivers in Sierra Leone) pay through fuel costs; rural households pay through goods prices. The CPAT incidence module quantifies these effects; the political-economy reading is that fuel-tax opposition tends to be loudest among informal-sector transport workers, whose visibility in the capital is high relative to their share of the affected population. Compensation design needs to address them explicitly — fuel-card schemes, route-licence concessions, or direct cash transfers via mobile money — not just generic household transfers.

On the structural side, the redenomination anomaly in Sierra Leonean wine excise persists because nobody loses from its persistence. Wine importers and consumers face a near-zero rate; the Treasury loses revenue that was never accounted for; no organised constituency campaigns for restoration. Reform is therefore easy in the technical sense (a one-line amendment) and easy in the political sense (no loser is mobilised against it) but requires Treasury attention to surface in the first place. The diagnostic is what surfaces it.

### C4.2 Why diesel is harder than gasoline

Part B's Section 4 found that diesel is substantially undertaxed for externalities while gasoline is roughly correctly taxed. This is the textbook finding for developing countries. It is also the textbook political problem.

Gasoline is consumed predominantly by private passenger vehicles, which are predominantly owned by upper-quintile households. A gasoline-tax increase is mildly progressive on direct incidence. Diesel is consumed predominantly by trucks, buses and informal-sector vehicles. A diesel-tax increase is approximately distribution-neutral on direct incidence because the effect transmits through goods prices and fares to all households. But the political incidence is different from the economic incidence. Diesel-tax increases are visible to truck drivers, bus owners and informal-transport operators — three of the most politically mobilisable groups in most African capitals. Gasoline-tax increases are visible to a smaller, less mobilised constituency.

The implication for sequencing: a diesel-tax reform announced alone, without recycling and without the road-safety framing, is politically high-risk. A diesel-tax reform announced alongside a per-household transfer, with the road-safety framing prominent, and ideally bundled with a gasoline increase so that the visible signal is “fuel prices are going up” rather than “the government is targeting truckers”, has a much better track record. Rwanda, Ghana and Kenya all bundled.

### C4.3 Why tobacco is easier in some countries than others

Tobacco-tax increases face minimal organised opposition in countries with no domestic production. Sierra Leone imports all tobacco; the only domestic constituency is the smoking population itself, which is small (3 to 5 per cent of adults). The phased path from USD 0.14 per pack toward Uganda's lowest tier of USD 0.35 — three Finance Acts at plus 30 per cent each — is therefore politically straightforward. The fiscal yield is small (the base is narrow) but the public-health case is strong and the opposition is minimal.

Uganda is different. Domestic tobacco production exists, including for export. Tobacco-tax increases there face an organised domestic constituency. The FA2025 doubling of imported-cigarette rates (UGX 75,000 to 150,000 per 1,000 sticks for soft cap, UGX 100,000 to 200,000 for hinge lid) without an equivalent increase on the locally manufactured tiers (55,000 to 65,000; 80,000 to 90,000) is recognisable as a political compromise: imports take the larger increase because domestic producers are politically organised. The diagnostic surfaces the discrimination without adjudicating it.

The implication for Part C is general: reforms that target imports take a different political path from reforms that affect domestic production. Country teams need to know which they are recommending.

### C4.4 Why SSB excise is politically tractable now

Sugar-sweetened beverage excise is unusual in being both fiscally material (in countries with a meaningful SSB base) and politically tractable. Five features matter.

- The international precedent is substantial. Mexico (2014), South Africa (2018), UK (2018), Saudi Arabia (2017), the Gulf states more broadly, the Philippines (2018), and Chile in modified form. A country considering an SSB excise is no longer the outlier.

- The public-health case is well-evidenced and well-communicated. Diabetes, obesity, and dental-health concerns translate readily into public-facing arguments.

- Domestic constituencies are mixed. Bottlers oppose; public-health advocates support; ministries of health are typically supportive partners; ministries of finance get revenue.

- Sugar-content graduation, on the UK SDIL model, gives manufacturers an incentive to reformulate rather than oppose, partially neutralising the bottler lobby.

- Implementation through the existing excise architecture is technically straightforward — both Uganda and Sierra Leone already tax some non-alcoholic beverages and would need only to graduate the rate by sugar content.

For Tier 2 countries running the diagnostic, SSB excise is therefore a high-priority candidate in the C5 reform pathway: it scores well on tractability, fiscal yield is moderate, public-health gains are well-evidenced, and the international precedent makes the comparator argument easy.

### C4.5 The framing question: health, safety, or climate?

Across LIC and weak-data LMIC settings, the climate framing polls poorly for fuel-tax reforms. The health and road-safety framing polls substantially better. Part B's externality decomposition shows why: in the Country X worked example, air pollution and accidents together account for 70 per cent of the implicit-subsidy gap, while carbon accounts for less than 20 per cent. The framing choice is therefore not a betrayal of the underlying logic but a recognition of the empirical magnitudes. Climate matters, but in LICs the air-pollution and accident magnitudes are larger and the political resonance of those framings is stronger.

Tier 1 settings differ. In countries with a more developed climate-policy debate (South Africa, Colombia, Chile, Mexico), the carbon framing can do real work. The diagnostic does not impose a single framing; it provides the decomposition that lets country teams make the framing decision deliberately.

### C4.6 Why the schedule itself encodes political-economy information

A subtle but important point: the structure of the schedule itself encodes political-economy information that is invisible to a reader who looks only at the rate. The four-band local-content beer regime is a political artefact. The differential treatment of imported and locally manufactured cigarettes is a political artefact. The cooking-oil rate untouched for a decade is a political artefact. The wine redenomination anomaly is a political artefact (of omission rather than commission). The Part A diagnostic — by laying out structure, differentiation and history on five fields — makes these artefacts legible. Part C reads them as political-economy data.

This reading has a practical implication for any country team running the diagnostic. The five-field structure of Part A is not just a documentation device; it is a political-economy instrument. A line that has been amended every year is a politically active line. A line untouched for a decade is a politically inactive line — usually because no organised constituency benefits from changing it. A line carrying a local-content discount is a producer-protection line in fiscal clothing. A line carrying an origin or import distinction is an industrial-policy line. The diagnostic's job is not to adjudicate these political-economy choices but to surface them clearly enough that they can be addressed deliberately.

# C5. A sequenced reform pathway

Drawing together the Part A and Part B candidates, the comparator experience in C3, and the political-economy reading in C4, the reform pathway below sequences candidates by political tractability, fiscal yield, and administrative readiness. The pathway is templated rather than universal: in any given country, the candidates would be adjusted to local data. The structure — three years, one anchor reform per year, with smaller reforms layered alongside — is intended as a default.

### C5.1 The three-year package

  --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  **Year**     **Anchor reform**                                                                                                                                                                                           **Companion reforms**                                                                                                                                        **Yield / framing**
  ------------ ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  **Year 1**   Diesel-tax closure, step 1 (e.g. USD 0.15 / litre). Recycling design announced simultaneously: 30 per cent of new revenue into a flat per-household transfer through existing social-protection channels.   Tobacco rate increase (where domestic production is absent or weak); wine redenomination (where applicable); first move on SSB graduation.                   Approximately 0.3 to 0.5 per cent of GDP at full step. Framing: health and road safety, not climate.

  **Year 2**   Diesel-tax closure, step 2 (further USD 0.15 / litre). Per-household transfer institutionalised as a permanent indexed component of the social safety net.                                                  Emissions-and-weight feebate on imported vehicles. Full sugar-content-graduated SSB excise (e.g. UK SDIL design). Indexation of specific rates introduced.   Additional approximately 0.3 to 0.4 per cent of GDP. Framing: revenue stability and fleet modernisation.

  **Year 3**   Diesel-tax closure, step 3 (USD 0.20 / litre). Closes roughly two-thirds of the original gap.                                                                                                               Scoping of distance-based heavy-goods-vehicle charge. Diagnostic update with new exposure and accident data.                                                 Final approximately 0.3 to 0.4 per cent of GDP. Framing: international convergence and CBAM exposure management.
  --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The package raises an estimated 0.9 to 1.3 per cent of GDP in additional revenue at full implementation. The bottom quintile is better off in net terms once the per-household transfer is in place. The implicit-subsidy gap is approximately halved; full closure would require complementary instruments beyond fuel taxation (heavy-goods-vehicle charges, urban congestion pricing, vehicle-stock turnover policy). These are flagged for a future diagnostic update rather than for the current cycle.

### C5.2 Country-specific tailoring

The three-year template adapts to country-specific findings from Parts A and B. Three illustrative tailorings:

- **Uganda.** Anchor diesel reform is supportable (Uganda runs closer to OECD intensity than Sierra Leone but still substantially below). SSB graduation is high priority (flat 12 per cent or UGX 250 per litre is the largest gap to peers). Tobacco reform is harder in year one because domestic production is politically organised; the FA2025 discrimination between locally manufactured and imported tiers is the workable path. Indexation should be introduced in year two given the long erosion-and-restoration history visible in Appendix B.

- **Sierra Leone.** Wine redenomination is the year-one transparency win. Tobacco rate convergence toward Uganda's lowest tier is politically straightforward (no domestic production). SSB excise needs to be introduced from a low base — currently only energy drinks and imported juice are taxed. Diesel reform is fiscally material (current 18 per cent of pump price has more headroom than Uganda's 30 per cent) but requires the recycling design to be in place first.

- **Tier 1 settings (Colombia, Chile, South Africa).** Anchor reform shifts from diesel-tax closure (which is closer to its corrective rate) toward the carbon component on fuels. The framing shifts from health and safety toward climate, supported by the more developed domestic climate-policy debate. Vehicle-stock vintage modelling becomes essential. The compensation design uses more sophisticated targeting through existing tax-credit infrastructure rather than flat per-household transfers.

### C5.3 What the pathway does not attempt

Three reforms regularly raised in the externality literature are deliberately not included as anchors in the three-year package. They are flagged here as candidates for a longer reform horizon.

- **Comprehensive carbon tax.** A standalone carbon tax covering multiple sectors is institutionally more demanding than a carbon component on fuels and faces a steeper political hurdle. Most LICs would do better to introduce a carbon component on fuels first and broaden later. The diagnostic flags the comprehensive instrument as a longer-term direction rather than a three-year reform.

- **Congestion pricing.** Administratively demanding; politically contentious; well-suited only to a small number of larger cities. The diagnostic notes congestion as a known externality but does not include congestion pricing in the three-year package for most countries.

- **Full vehicle-stock turnover policy.** A coordinated package of import duties, age-based registration fees, scrappage incentives and emissions standards is the right answer to the vehicle-stock problem in the long run. In the three-year package, the feebate is the first move; the rest takes longer.

# C6. Conclusion of Part C

Part C's contribution is sequencing. The substantive findings come from Parts A and B; the comparator references come from the international and national-practice review in Part B (sections B2 and B3); the political-economy reading comes from the schedule and externality decomposition themselves, not from new analysis. Part C's value is in joining these inputs together into a reform pathway that survives contact with politics.

Three observations close the section. First, the reform pathway is not normative. It is templated. Country teams running the diagnostic can — and should — depart from the template where local conditions warrant. The discipline is in the inputs (the Part A and Part B findings, the comparator references, the political-economy reading) rather than in the output (the three-year sequence).

Second, the pathway is incremental rather than transformative. None of the year-one reforms is structurally novel; all are extensions of existing schedule architecture or implementations of designs proven in comparator countries. This is by design. Transformative reforms have a poor track record in LIC settings; incremental reforms with strong recycling and clear framing have a better one.

Third, the pathway is a starting point for country dialogue, not a finished product. The diagnostic does not negotiate compensation packages, draft Finance Bills, or design social-protection delivery infrastructure. It identifies which reforms are tractable, in what sequence, with what comparator backing. The rest is the work of the country team and its government counterparts.

# Next steps

Moving from concept to product does not require building the whole three-part diagnostic at once. The two parts sit at very different levels of readiness, and the sensible path is to ship the part that is ready and to integrate the part that is not into processes that already exist.

## Start with a simplified Part A

Part A is the immediate opportunity. It needs no new modelling capacity, no new valuation parameters, and no cross-team data exchange: it is the disciplined reading of an excise schedule that the two pilots (Uganda and Sierra Leone) already demonstrate. A simplified Part A could be standardised and rolled out quickly with a light apparatus.

- **A fixed template and parameter sheet.** Codify the five recording fields and the three comparable measures (\$/unit, % of consumer price, % of GDP) in a Word template populated from a single parameter spreadsheet — working exchange rates, representative prices, volumes and the GDP denominator — so a country team fills inputs rather than rebuilding the method.

- **A minimum viable diagnostic.** For a first pass, require only the questions that the schedule alone can answer — coverage, structure, intensity and erosion (Q1–Q3, Q5). Benchmarking and coherence (Q4, Q6) and price tracking (Q7) are added as data allow, matching the “required” versus “case-dependent” split in the PFR table in the executive summary.

- **Reuse the pilots as worked models.** The Uganda and Sierra Leone diagnostics serve as templates; a third country should be reproducible in two to three weeks rather than months.

- **A shared tool inventory and a light visualisation.** List the analytical tools held by the climate and health teams on the excise-tax section of the website and, if feasible, surface the standardised Part A measures through a simple dashboard (a Power BI page or a PFR Visualisation Tool input) rather than a bespoke build.

## Part B requires deeper integration with existing processes

Part B is not a quick rollout. Its value comes precisely from harmonising outputs that today live in separate programs — CPAT, the Climate and Health Program, IMF Getting Energy Prices Right — onto one valuation spine, and that harmonisation is an institutional task as much as an analytical one. Several of its key questions (Q8–Q23) can only be answered by drawing on data and models held by other teams.

- **Agree the valuation spine across teams.** A single value of statistical life, a single carbon shadow price and a single accident-cost set must be fixed once and adopted by all contributing teams — the discipline that gives the report its consistency.

- **Connect to CPAT and the Climate and Health Program as input pipelines.** Part B ingests rather than re-computes: incidence from the CPAT module, mortality and exposure from the Climate and Health Program, corrective-rate benchmarks from IMF GEPR. Each needs an agreed hand-off.

- **Settle the equity and tooling questions.** Confirm which household surveys can be reopened for health-tax incidence (feasible for tobacco and alcohol; SSBs may not be separable), and whether the joint output is delivered as a Power BI website or a PFR Visualisation Tool input.

- **Sequence Part B behind a Part A pilot.** A natural order is to ship simplified Part A first, then layer Part B for the Tier 1 pilot (Colombia or Chile) and the Tier 2 pilot (Uganda) once the input pipelines and the valuation spine are in place.

In short: Part A can be simplified and shipped on its own; Part B should be built into the existing climate and health workflows rather than bolted on. Appendix D sets out, capacity by capacity, what each program already holds and where in this report the corresponding question is addressed.

# Appendix A. The full diagnostics

Both diagnostics use the five-column structure described in section A3.3. The structure-and-differentiation column compresses three of the five fields. Rows are organised by the seven-category typology of section A3.2.

# Appendix B. Recent changes, year by year

This appendix documents the year-by-year changes that produced the current law shown in Appendix A. For each country, it begins with the starting position at the start of 2020 and tracks the substantive amendments in each Finance Act (Sierra Leone) or Excise Duty Amendment Act (Uganda) through to the most recent enacted instrument. Pending bills are flagged separately.

## B.1 Uganda

### Starting position: FY 2019/20, before the Excise Duty (Amendment) Act, 2020

The schedule at the start of 2020 reflected accumulated amendments through Act 12 of 2019. The main lines were as follows. Tobacco: specific rates by pack type and origin — locally manufactured soft cap UGX 55,000 per 1,000 sticks, imported soft cap UGX 75,000; locally manufactured hinge lid UGX 80,000, imported hinge lid UGX 100,000. Cigars and other tobacco at 200% ad valorem. Alcohol: malt beer 60% or UGX 2,050/litre; beer with ≥75% local raw material 30% or UGX 650/litre; opaque beer 30% or UGX 650/litre; un-denatured spirits from local raw materials 60% or UGX 2,000/litre; from imported raw materials 100% or UGX 2,500/litre. Fuel: petrol UGX 1,200/litre; diesel UGX 880/litre; kerosene UGX 200/litre. Telecommunications: 12% on airtime, with a separate UGX 200/day OTT (over-the-top) social-media levy outside the Schedule. Financial services: 0.5% on mobile money cash withdrawals, 15% on bank ledger and ATM fees.

### Excise Duty (Amendment) Act, 2020 (Act 21/2020, effective 1 July 2020)

- Petrol: UGX 1,200 → 1,350/litre. Diesel: UGX 880 → 1,030/litre.

- Un-denatured spirits from local raw materials: UGX 2,000 → 1,500/litre (60% rate retained).

- Fruit and vegetable juice: UGX 300 → 250/litre.

- COVID-19 measures: nil rate on un-denatured spirits used for sanitiser / disinfectant production (≥75% alcohol content); plastic bag duty introduced at UGX 10,000/kg with sanitary-pad and food / juice / tea / coffee packaging exemptions.

### Excise Duty (Amendment) Acts, 2021 (Acts 6 and 16/2021, effective 1 July 2021)

- Petrol: 1,350 → 1,450/litre. Diesel: 1,030 → 1,130/litre.

- OTT levy repealed; replaced by 12% excise on internet data, with medical and education data exempted.

- Opaque beer cut from 30% or UGX 650/litre to 20% or UGX 230/litre.

- “Any other locally produced alcoholic beverage” brought in at 20% or UGX 230/litre — formalising tax on Kombucha, Kaziire, etc.

- New line: other fermented beverages (cider, perry, mead, near beer) — 60% or UGX 950/litre imported; 30% or UGX 550/litre locally grown.

### Excise Duty (Amendment) Act, 2022

Largely an inflation-adjustment package. Parliament rejected an opposition proposal to cut petrol back to UGX 750/litre. Fuel rates held at 1,450/1,130. Minor rate corrections elsewhere; no major new excisable items.

### Excise Duty (Amendment) Acts, 2023 (Acts 17/2023 and 24/2023)

- Definitions added for fruit juice, un-denatured spirits, vegetable juice.

- Equivalent treatment for Islamic financial business: ledger / ATM / transaction charges placed on the same 15% footing as conventional banking.

- Schedule 2 varied for opaque beer, undenatured spirits, fruit / vegetable juice, certain construction materials, certain non-alcoholic beverages.

### Excise Duty (Amendment) Act, 2024 (effective 1 July 2024)

- Petrol: 1,450 → 1,550/litre. Diesel: 1,130 → 1,230/litre.

- Un-denatured spirits and “other wine” rates increased.

- Opaque beer and other locally produced alcoholic beverages cut further: “any other locally produced alcoholic beverage” 20% or UGX 230 → 12% or UGX 150/litre.

- New definitions: powder for reconstitution into beer.

- New excisable items: powder for reconstitution into beer; payment services (cash withdrawal via agent banking, Chipper Cash, Wave) at 0.5% — equalising treatment with mobile money.

- International calls from Burundi and Tanzania removed from the USD 0.09/min charge.

- Construction materials for EV manufacturers and EV parts / accessories exempted.

- Mineral water duty restructured to fixed-and-ad-valorem hybrid.

### Excise Duty (Amendment) Acts, 2025 — No. 1 and No. 2 (effective 1 July 2025)

- Cigarettes (first significant change since FY 2017/18): locally manufactured soft cap 55,000 → 65,000; imported soft cap 75,000 → 150,000 (doubled); locally manufactured hinge lid 80,000 → 90,000; imported hinge lid 100,000 → 200,000 (doubled).

- Beer from local raw material (≥75%): UGX 650 → 900/litre (rate 30% retained).

- New Section 13A: framework for remission of excise duty on damaged, expired or obsolete goods.

- Originally proposed petrol increase to UGX 1,650 and diesel to UGX 1,380 was rescinded by the Minister of Finance before passage; fuel rates remained at 1,550 / 1,230.

- Other revisions to fruit juice, motor fuel categories and plastic products in line with the Bill's revenue-and-base-broadening logic.

### Pending: Excise Duty (Amendment) Bill, 2026

The Bill was passed by Parliament in late April 2026 but, as of the cut-off date of this paper, had not received presidential assent and is therefore not in force. Notable proposed changes (intended effective date 1 July 2026): petrol +UGX 200/litre (1,550 → 1,750), diesel to roughly 1,430, sugar 100 → 300/kg, cement to 750/50kg (down from a proposed 1,000), imported spirits to UGX 3,500/litre or 80%, motorcycles first registration 200,000 → 500,000, plastics from 2.5% / USD 70 per tonne to 25% / USD 1,500 per tonne with the base widened to disposable cups, straws, bottles and stirrers, a new excise on cooking fat at UGX 500/litre or kg.

## B.2 Sierra Leone

### Starting position: at 1 January 2020 (post-FA2020)

Tobacco: 30% ad valorem on the wholesale price of cigarettes (introduced through the FA2018 reform) plus elevated import duties on all tobacco products. Alcohol: specific excise of USD 1.5/litre on alcoholic beverages of up to 10% ABV, USD 2/litre above 10% ABV — applied uniformly to imports and most domestic production. Soft drinks: energy drinks at 20%; excise also on bottled and processed water. Fuel: specific excise on petrol, diesel, kerosene, fuel oil and lubricating oils under tariff item 27.10 (rates inherited from earlier Finance Acts). FA2020 itself: added a single new line — imported fruit and vegetable juice at 20%. Telecommunications and financial services: not subject to excise duty under the 1982 Act. Telecom services within the GST net at 15%; financial services GST-exempt.

### Finance Act, 2021 (effective 1 January 2021)

- First major re-engineering of the alcohol regime. Tariff item 22.09 repealed and replaced with a four-band local-content beer regime: D1 (\>80% local) 5%; D2 (\>70%, \<80%) 8%; D3 (\>60%, \<70%) 12%; D4 (\>50%, \<60%) 15%.

- Eligible local raw materials defined as sorghum, cassava, maize, sugar and barley.

- Vegetable oils, palm olein and margarine added at 10% (heading 15.11).

- Soaps at 20% (heading 34.01).

- Industrial fatty-acid oils at 20% (heading 38.23).

- Nails at 5% (heading 73.17).

### Finance Act, 2022 (effective 1 January 2022)

No Schedule-level excise changes. The Act focused on income tax (cut petroleum operations from 30% to 25%), taxpayer segmentation, and digital-marketplace definitions in GST. Excise rates from FA2021 carried forward.

### Finance Act, 2023

Imposed a new set of regulatory levies on telecommunications operators (sometimes labelled “excise” colloquially but legally a separate levy under the Finance Act, not under the Excise Act): on-net mobile voice calls Le 0.1/minute; off-net Le 0.05/minute; outgoing international calls Le 0.2/minute; mobile money commissions 2%; mobile data up to 5% of recharge / bundle value.

### Finance Act, 2024 (effective 1 January 2024)

The most substantial single-Act re-write of the schedule in the period.

- Imported cement to 20%. Iron rod 10%. Cooking gas 5%. Rice graduated from 0 to 5% then 10% from 2025.

- Beer (heading 22.03) restructured: malt beer, stout, porter, non-alcoholic beer (≤5%) and “other” all at Le 0.01/cl or Le 10/litre local; Le 0.015/cl or Le 15/litre import.

- Wine (headings 22.04, 22.05) rebanded by ABV: Le 4.20/litre (≤10%), Le 6.30 (\>10–20%), Le 8.30 (\>20–30%), Le 10.40 (\>30–40%), Le 15.0 (\>40%) for local; Le 10/12/14/16/22/litre for imports along the same bands.

- Cigarettes restructured under tariff items 24.01–24.03 (specific tobacco rates per kg and per packet).

- Electronic cigarettes and cartridges introduced at item 24.04: Le 0.2/ml device, Le 0.4/unit cartridge.

- Fuel rates set at Le 0.81/litre kerosene, Le 2.80/litre petrol, Le 1.22/litre diesel rising on a published quarterly schedule to Le 2.40/litre by 1 October 2024, Le 4.14/litre fuel oil, Le 2.20/litre lubricating oils.

- Plastics: polyethylene bags and plastic bottles (with beverage, excluding water) at Le 16/kg.

- New excise on gambling, betting and lottery services at 10% of net wagered (gross gambling revenue less winnings) — inserted at item 98.01.

### Finance Act, 2025 (effective 1 January 2025)

First Finance Act in fully redenominated New Leone units. Two structural additions: section 5 (21-day excise payment rule) and section 48A (filing of excise returns with graduated penalties for large / medium / small taxpayers).

- Beer regime (item 22.09) re-tiered: D1 (\>80% local) at 5/8/12% across \<10, 10–20, ≥20 ABV; D2 (\>70–80%) at 8/12/15%; D3 (\>60–70%) at 12/15/17.5%; D4 (\>30–60%) at 15/17.5/20%. The local-content threshold for D4 widened from 50–60% to 30–60%, bringing more producers into the higher band.

- Tobacco (24.01–24.04) restated in NLe: unmanufactured tobacco NLe 65/kg; cigars and cigarillos NLe 25/packet; cigarettes NLe 2/packet of 20 sticks; other manufactured tobacco NLe 65/kg; shisha and herbal molasses NLe 65/kg + NLe 175/litre; e-cigarette device NLe 0.5/ml; cartridge NLe 0.8/unit.

### Finance Act, 2026 (effective 1 January 2026)

The latest enacted Finance Act. Tobacco and fuel re-tariffed upward, and cement re-stated.

- Cigarettes: rate raised to NLe 3/packet of 20 sticks (50% up from FA2025's NLe 2).

- Cigars / cigarillos: NLe 38/packet (up from NLe 25, \~52%).

- Unmanufactured tobacco / other manufactured tobacco: NLe 98/kg (up from NLe 65, \~51%).

- Shisha / hookah / vaping alternatives: NLe 98/kg + NLe 225/litre.

- E-cigarettes: NLe 0.75/ml device; NLe 1.20/unit cartridge (50% each).

- Cement (item 25.23): Portland, slag, super-sulphate and other hydraulic cement at NLe 10/50 kg bag.

- Fuel (item 27.10) restated in NLe: kerosene NLe 2/litre; petrol NLe 5/litre; diesel NLe 5/litre; fuel oil NLe 7.40/litre; lubricating oils NLe 4/litre.

- New annual circulation levy on vehicles (NLe 500 for ordinary cars / trucks / buses; USD 1,000 / 500 for large vessels and water taxis depending on capacity; NLe 200 for motorbikes), payable at importation, registration or licensing — structurally outside the Excise Act but fiscally adjacent.

Read together, the two recent-changes histories show three common patterns. Both countries used the 2020 amendment cycle for selective COVID-related concessions and modest fuel-rate rises. Both used the 2021 amendment cycle to re-engineer the alcohol regime around local-content discounts. Both used the 2024 amendment cycle to broaden the base — Sierra Leone introducing e-cigarettes, gambling and plastic bottles; Uganda introducing payment services and powder-for-reconstitution-into-beer. Both have used the 2025 and 2026 cycles primarily for inflation catch-up — the cigarette-rate increases in both countries, the fuel restatements in Sierra Leone, the proposed fuel and motorcycle increases in Uganda's pending 2026 Bill.
